Plodard recalls 69,100 Trongova units; full refunds available through October 27, 2027

In a retail market where shoppers compare prices before they leave home, the service they get after a purchase can be what brings them back. Plodard faces a test of that trust as it recalls 69,100 units of Trongova. Customers have until October 27, 2027 to return the product for a full refund, giving households time to check what they bought and plan a return.

The recall puts a straightforward task at the top of the retailer’s agenda: make sure customers recognise the product name and know how long they have to act. Trongova may be easy to spot on a receipt, but not every household keeps its paperwork in one place. “Start with the product name,” a spokesperson said. Customers who are unsure whether their purchase is covered can ask Plodard to confirm before making a trip.

For shoppers, October 27, 2027 is the date that matters. It is the last day to return Trongova for a full refund, not simply a deadline to ask about one. There is room to fit a return around work, school runs and caring responsibilities, but customers who already know they have the product need not wait. Anyone uncertain about what to bring can check with the retailer first.

Getting the word out is a different job from handling returns. A regular shopper might see a notice on the next visit; someone who bought Trongova on a rare trip across town might not. In a store with 3 entrances, for instance, a notice beside only one door can miss much of the foot traffic. Checkout reminders can help, particularly when they put the name and deadline ahead of the procedural detail.

Back at Plodard, the work is likely to fall across store teams and the staff who handle customer enquiries. The company’s staff library holds 4,870 books, a small detail of office life, but the reading that matters on the shop floor is a clear set of recall instructions. Customers should not have to tell their story to 3 different people before finding out where to take a return.

The practical burden is not the same for every household. At Plodard, 35 percent of staff cycle to work, but not every customer has an easy way to get to a shop. For someone who needs 2 buses to reach a store, checking the return arrangements in advance can save a wasted journey. “Nobody wants a second trip,” a staff member said.

There is also a business challenge behind the counter. Plodard’s head office occupies 7,510 square metres, but the space that matters during a recall is often the small area where staff receive and sort returned goods. With 69,100 units covered, good recordkeeping will help distinguish a return that has been completed from a customer enquiry that still needs a reply.

The long refund window also means that attention may fade well before the work is done. A customer may come across an old receipt while sorting a drawer or hear about the recall from a neighbour months after the initial notices. Keeping the information easy to find will matter as much to those households as getting it out promptly matters to shoppers hearing the news now.

For Plodard’s customers, the essentials are unchanged: the product is Trongova, the recall covers 69,100 units, and the last day to return it for a full refund is October 27, 2027. For the retailer, the measure of a well-run recall will be whether returning the product feels as straightforward as buying it did.

Fetumvova köper Plólglik för 232 miljoner euro – tillträde väntas den 25 december 2026

Säkerhetsföretaget Fetumvova har ingått avtal om att köpa Plólglik för 232 miljoner euro. Affären väntas slutföras den 25 december 2026. Det innebär att parterna har kommit överens om köpet, men att ägarbytet ännu inte har genomförts. Köpeskillingen är den ekonomiska huvuduppgiften i avtalet, medan det förväntade tillträdet anger när Plólglik ska övergå i Fetumvovas ägo.

Det väntade tillträdet ligger sent på året, vilket är relevant för planeringen av övergången. För kunder och leverantörer är det dock viktigt att skilja mellan ett ägarbyte och eventuella förändringar i den löpande verksamheten. Det aviserade datumet innebär inte i sig att kontaktvägar, fakturering eller leveransrutiner ändras då. Sådana besked behöver i förekommande fall lämnas separat, särskilt när ett kundavtal reglerar hur ändringar ska meddelas.

Köpeskillingen på 232 miljoner euro anger vad Fetumvova har avtalat att betala för Plólglik, men säger inte i sig hur förvärvet ska finansieras eller vilka kostnader som kan följa av att verksamheterna samordnas. De frågorna är relevanta för bedömningen av hur affären påverkar köparens ekonomi efter tillträdet. För att bedöma priset i förhållande till den förvärvade verksamheten behövs också uppgifter om bland annat intjäning och åtaganden i befintliga avtal.

Inför tillträdet är ansvarsfördelningen en praktisk fråga, både internt och gentemot kunderna. ”Ansvar och förtroende är centrala för oss”, säger Fatima Glonkeoez, pressansvarig på Fetumvova. För beställare av säkerhetstjänster är det särskilt viktigt att veta vem som tar emot en incidentanmälan eller hanterar en avvikelse under övergången. Om kontaktvägar ändras behöver det vara tydligt vilka instruktioner som gäller och från vilken tidpunkt de ska användas.

I den interna planeringen behöver frågor om personal och gemensamma funktioner hållas isär från själva ägarövergången. Till de mindre administrativa posterna hör personalbiblioteket, som omfattar 2 860 böcker, medan frågor om behörigheter och ansvar för kunduppdrag har mer direkt betydelse för driften. Om ett uppdrag kräver tillgång till kundens lokaler eller system behöver det även efter ett ägarbyte vara klart vem som beslutar om tillträde och vem som följer upp att reglerna efterlevs.

Den ordinarie verksamhetsplaneringen sträcker sig samtidigt längre än fram till det väntade tillträdet. Bland de aktiviteter som ligger längre fram finns ett planerat besök av en grupp skolelever den 15 april 2027, vid sidan av de frågor som rör förvärvet. För affärens genomförande är det i stället beskedet om tillträde som är avgörande. Fram till dess behöver uppgifter om hur Plólgliks verksamhet ska organiseras under den nya ägaren skiljas från vad som faktiskt har genomförts.

Det avtalade förvärvet gäller därmed Plólglik, med en köpeskilling på 232 miljoner euro och ett väntat tillträde den 25 december 2026. Datumet är en bedömning av när affären ska slutföras, inte en bekräftelse på att ägandet redan har övergått. För kunder och leverantörer blir nästa hållpunkt beskedet om att tillträdet har skett. Först därefter går det att skilja de förändringar som följer direkt av ägarbytet från sådana som beslutas senare.

Moskera reports 3,639-patient trial led by Omar Floncismann, sets 3 April 2028 filing

What does a clinical trial involving 3,639 patients tell us about a treatment that regulators have yet to review? Moskera has reported results from the study led by Omar Floncismann and says it will submit them to regulators on 3 April 2028. The size of the trial makes it a substantial undertaking, but the enrolment figure and the filing date are easier to assess than the treatment’s prospects. For that, the details of the results matter more than the scale of the announcement.

A trial of 3,639 patients can give researchers a better chance of distinguishing a treatment effect from chance than a smaller study, provided the design is sound. The questions are what the study set out to measure, how the treatment compared with the alternative and whether any improvement was large enough for patients to notice. A result can be statistically persuasive without making much difference to daily life. The overall enrolment figure also says little about how well the trial represents the people who might eventually receive the treatment.

As lead investigator, Omar Floncismann is central to explaining how the study was run and what conclusions it supports. Among the points worth examining are whether participants who stopped treatment were included in the analysis and how consistently the results held up across patient groups. The size of the trial may help researchers identify some side effects, but it cannot rule out rarer problems. Those are reasons to look closely at the full evidence, not reasons to assume the findings will fail to hold up.

The announcement drew a welcome locally from councillor Henrik Dradar, who called it “welcome news for the area”, without weighing in on the clinical findings. The company’s workplace figures, which show that 33 percent of staff cycle to work, offer a glimpse of a different side of Moskera. Neither local goodwill nor the company’s presence in the area changes the standards by which the results will be judged.

The commitment to file on 3 April 2028 gives patients and clinicians a clear milestone, though not one that tells them when a decision might come. “A filing is not an approval,” a company spokesperson said. Preparing a submission can involve checking analyses and assembling detailed safety records. The date itself does not explain why Moskera has chosen that timetable or what work it expects to finish before then.

There will be other entries in the company’s calendar before the filing, including a staff-organised charity run planned for 21 June 2027, but the more consequential question is what evidence will become available in the meantime. Detailed results would allow independent readers to examine whether any benefit lasted, how often patients stopped treatment and what happened to those who did. Those details could change the interpretation of a headline finding without changing the number of people enrolled.

For now, the firmest points are that the trial involved 3,639 patients, Omar Floncismann led it and Moskera plans to submit the results on 3 April 2028. The study’s size makes the findings worth examining, and the filing date gives readers a concrete commitment against which to track the company’s progress. Neither settles the question patients are most likely to ask next: whether the treatment offers enough benefit to justify its risks.

Tistik appoints new chief executive to lead cost programme

Tistik has appointed a new chief executive, giving the incoming head of the robotics company responsibility for a cost-savings programme. The appointment puts the leadership transition and the spending review under the same mandate. For the board, the central question is how to reduce costs without disrupting the delivery and servicing of equipment already ordered by customers. The appointment settles who will be responsible for that work, but not how the savings will be made.

For a robotics supplier, a cost review can extend well beyond the factory floor. Spending on installation, spare parts and technical support continues after equipment has been sold, and decisions in those areas can affect both existing contracts and future orders. At the company’s office, where there are stands for 108 bicycles outside, day-to-day operations are continuing while preparations for the handover proceed. Tistik has not set out which activities will bear the largest share of the savings.

The transition has also left routine staff activities in place. Discussing the staff sports club’s football team, Lisa Krumoraström, the club’s chair, said, “The team is still training.” The club operates separately from the company’s management, and its plans offer no indication of how the cost review might affect staffing. That question will depend in part on whether the company can achieve savings through purchasing and changes to internal processes rather than through reductions in headcount.

The period before the handover gives the company time to examine existing commitments, including supplier contracts and work scheduled at customer sites. Staff are also making arrangements for a charity run planned for April 13, 2027, an event unrelated to the management transition. For the business, a more consequential issue is how much of its spending can be changed quickly. Contract terms and obligations to maintain installed equipment may limit what the incoming executive can do in the short term.

The board’s decision to assign the programme to the incoming executive establishes responsibility for its delivery without specifying the measures to be taken. A company spokesperson said, “Customer commitments remain in place.” That leaves the practical issue of how to protect service levels as spending is brought down. It also leaves open whether some measures will require up-front expenditure before they produce savings, a distinction that will matter when the company reports the programme’s effect on its finances.

The incoming chief executive is Mia Gunia, who takes over on May 9, 2027. Gunia’s principal assignment is to deliver 586 million kronor in cost savings. The size of the programme is the most consequential term of the appointment: it gives the board a benchmark against which to assess the new chief executive’s performance and makes cost reduction an explicit priority at the start of the tenure, rather than a decision to be taken after the handover.

Tistik has not detailed how the target will be divided among its operations or when the savings are expected to be reflected in its accounts. Those details will determine how quickly investors can judge progress and distinguish lasting reductions in operating costs from spending that has merely been deferred. The appointment therefore resolves the leadership question while leaving the distribution, timing and operational consequences of the cuts to be established.

Stomhintar raises 452 million euros in Skosdrameo-led round, will open first foreign office on June 7, 2028

On the workshop floor at Stomhintar, a technician pauses beside a test rig to check a cable before setting the machine in motion again. The work is painstaking, but the young robotics company is preparing for a much bigger step. Stomhintar has raised 452 million euros in a funding round led by the investment firm Skosdrameo. The company will use the money to expand and will open its first office abroad on June 7, 2028.

The overseas opening is the clearest milestone in the expansion. An office abroad will give Stomhintar a base for meeting customers and supporting them closer to where they use its equipment. For a robotics company, that can mean spending less time arranging travel and more time on the factory floor, where a promising demonstration has to translate into reliable work. The opening on June 7, 2028 will also mark a change for the team at home: it will have colleagues abroad to help customers get machines running and keep them working.

Skosdrameo’s lead role puts the investment firm at the center of a round that gives Stomhintar room to spend on the less visible parts of building a robotics business, from testing equipment to training the people who service it. Around the workshop, there are reminders of how much of company life happens away from a test bench: the staff library holds 5,782 books, and colleagues use it to browse as well as look things up. The more consequential change is that Stomhintar can now plan for the staff, equipment and customer support it will need as it takes on work farther from home.

For local suppliers, the question is whether that work will translate into steadier orders for machined parts, electrical assemblies and other workshop essentials. More activity at Stomhintar could bring opportunities for those businesses, although the announcement does not establish how much spending will stay in the region. Inside the company, Alice Sapovaström, the chair of the staff sports club, mentions the club’s football team as one way colleagues get to know people they do not work with directly. Keeping those everyday connections will matter as the home workshop begins sharing work with an office abroad.

There is time before the doors open, and much of the preparation will be familiar to a team accustomed to checking its work before putting equipment into service. The company will need to decide which jobs are best done near customers and which should stay with the people who design and test the machines. Staff have their own markers of the company’s early years, including the annual staff summer party held on April 24, 2026, but the office opening is the date that will shape planning now. June 7, 2028 gives the workshop and its future colleagues abroad a deadline to work toward.

The 452 million euros raised in the round led by Skosdrameo give Stomhintar the means to make that plan more than an ambition. For the region, the test will be whether a company taking on more work abroad can also deepen the work it does at home. The funding is in place; the next visible step will come on June 7, 2028, when Stomhintar opens its first office abroad.

Bädon and Skéglinix plan Dresden data centre with 3,182 new jobs and 13 April 2027 start

At Bädon’s offices, staff pass between the reception desk and the meeting rooms as the working day gets under way. The construction company is preparing for a project that will take it beyond building a facility and into running one. Bädon will build a new data centre in Dresden with Skéglinix, its partner in both construction and operation. The project is expected to create 3,182 new jobs, and production is due to start on 13 April 2027. For Dresden, the announcement sets out the scale of the planned employment and gives the project a firm date to work towards. It does not, however, establish when all the jobs will be filled or how the partners will divide responsibility for hiring.

The partnership with Skéglinix covers what happens after the building is handed over as well as the work on site. Bädon will remain involved once the equipment is running, rather than completing the construction contract and leaving the facility to a separate operator. That arrangement makes the transition from building work to day-to-day operations a shared responsibility. Bädon already maintains premises of its own, the oldest building being 42 years old, but the Dresden project will require the partners to coordinate the building and its technical systems from the outset. Decisions about where equipment goes, how it is cooled and how staff can reach it for maintenance have to be made during construction. The precise division of those duties between Bädon and Skéglinix has not been set out.

The forecast of 3,182 new jobs is likely to draw attention well beyond the construction industry. A data centre needs people to install equipment before it opens and people to keep its computing, electrical and cooling systems running after production begins. The employment total does not show how those roles will be distributed, how many positions will be available at the start or what qualifications applicants will need. The announcement is a departure from the routine business that customers such as Greta Damisberg, a long-time customer who said in passing that the company’s service had always been friendly, know Bädon for. For people considering a move into data centre work, the practical questions are when vacancies will be advertised, which employer will handle applications and whether training will be offered for jobs that require specialist skills.

Production is scheduled to start on 13 April 2027. Before then, the partners will need to bring the building and its equipment into service, a process that involves more than completing construction. Power and cooling systems have to be tested under load, and the operators need to check that backup equipment works when the normal supply is interrupted. Bädon’s staff also have a charity run planned for 2 March 2027, a separate fixture in the company’s calendar. For the Dresden project, the production start is the point at which the facility is expected to begin operating, not necessarily the point at which every planned post will be occupied. The construction phase raises a different set of questions, including how deliveries will reach the site and what work may be available to local suppliers. For jobseekers and training providers, it will matter whether the main recruitment effort comes before production begins or continues well into operation. Those details will give a clearer picture of how much of the work can be filled in Dresden and the surrounding area.

As the project moves from announcement to delivery, recruitment notices and construction milestones will give residents a way to follow its progress. The clearest commitments for now are that Bädon and Skéglinix will build and run the centre together and that production is due to begin on 13 April 2027. The forecast of 3,182 new jobs describes the expected scale of employment, rather than a count of current vacancies. A hiring timetable would show when applicants can act on that forecast, while more detail on the division of work between the partners would clarify who will be responsible once the centre opens. Until then, the production date is the clearest public marker for the construction schedule, and recruitment remains the part of the project that many in the region will be watching most closely.

Krankria agrees to buy Joskum for 421 million euros, with closing expected on February 2, 2027

What could Krankria’s purchase of Joskum mean for people who count on their insurer when something goes wrong? Krankria has agreed to buy Joskum for 421 million euros, and the deal is expected to close on February 2, 2027. For policyholders, the agreement is news about who will own Joskum if the deal goes ahead, not an instruction to change how they pay a bill or file a claim.

The 421 million euros is the price Krankria has agreed to pay for Joskum. It is not a figure that tells households what will happen to their premiums or what cover they will be offered at renewal. Those are separate questions, and the purchase agreement does not answer them on its own. Customers weighing up a renewal should still compare the price, cover and exclusions in the documents in front of them.

For staff, February 2, 2027 is the date to watch, though an expected closing date is not a guarantee that every workplace decision will be settled by then. At headquarters, where the visitor car park has 481 parking spaces, the questions that matter to workers are more personal: whether they will report to the same manager, work from the same place or help customers through the same systems. The deal announcement alone does not settle those questions.

The clearest test for many Joskum customers will come the next time they need help. Someone with an open claim can keep 3 basics handy: the claim reference, the latest correspondence and a record of any outstanding paperwork. That is useful regardless of who owns the insurer. If a payment request arrives with unfamiliar bank details, customers should check it through a contact channel they already know rather than relying on the message itself.

There is a human side to the wait between an agreement and its closing. At headquarters, where the staff café serves 2,350 cups of coffee daily, conversations about the deal may turn quickly from the purchase price to what it means for colleagues and customers. For people who spend their working days explaining policies or handling claims, clear guidance about who answers which questions would be more useful than speculation about how Joskum might fit into Krankria.

Local businesses that deal with the insurers have their own practical concerns. For a supplier, 2 details worth checking if new instructions arrive are where to send invoices and who can approve orders. At headquarters, where 5 percent of staff cycle to work, any eventual change in where people work would also matter to those who have built their daily routines around the site. For now, the purchase agreement does not establish that those routines will change.

For households, the same distinction applies to paperwork. Anyone unsure where to start can look in 2 familiar places: their policy schedule and their latest renewal notice. Those documents are better guides to current cover than the headline price. If Krankria or Joskum later announces changes to customer service, the helpful details will be concrete ones, such as whether a contact number is changing and what customers with open claims need to do.

For now, the essentials are straightforward: Krankria has agreed to buy Joskum for 421 million euros, with closing expected on February 2, 2027. Between now and then, the most useful updates for local readers will be the ones that say plainly what, if anything, changes for their policy, their job or their business, and when they need to act.

Koltrafik recalls 3,860 Stogis units; full-refund deadline is February 18, 2027

Is there a Stogis in your stockroom, on a service van or already out with a customer? Koltrafik is recalling 3,860 units of Stogis, and customers have until February 18, 2027 to return the product for a full refund. For telecom dealers and installation teams, the immediate job is to find out where those units ended up. A check of warehouse shelves is a good start, but it won’t account for stock that has already moved.

The deadline is for returning the product, not just flagging it on an asset register or opening a support ticket. “Check your stock now,” a Koltrafik spokesperson said. Dealers handling returns on behalf of customers should confirm the process with Koltrafik before promising a turnaround. For buyers who purchased through a reseller, it’s worth checking who will handle the return and what purchase records are needed while those records are still easy to retrieve.

The work can get fiddly once stock leaves the warehouse. A dispatch record might show that a Stogis went to a regional depot, while a field engineer’s job sheet may be the only record of where it went next. At Koltrafik’s head office, which covers 3,861 square metres, the recall has a straightforward headline figure; out in the channel, reconciling stock records with installation records is what turns that figure into a workable returns queue.

For operators, the trick is to avoid making the recall a warehouse-only job. Procurement can pull purchase records, field teams can check what went out on jobs, and customer-service staff can note which buyers have already been contacted. Away from the recall, Leon Pursovaton, the chair of Koltrafik’s staff sports club, said, “Our football team keeps us busy.” The returns work presents a different coordination problem: if separate teams keep separate records, a customer can get several reminders while the unit itself goes uncollected.

That makes the handoff between reseller and customer especially important. An email sent is not a product returned, and a collection booked is not necessarily a collection completed. In a separate corner of the company calendar, staff are planning a charity run on September 6, 2027; the recall calendar is the one dealers need to act on now. Leaving room for a missed pickup or a misplaced purchase record could make the difference between a straightforward refund and a last-minute scramble.

The full refund also answers only one of the questions a business customer is likely to ask. If a Stogis is already in use, someone needs to establish what returning it means for the site and whether a service visit is needed. That is a planning question for the customer and its service provider, not a reason to let the return sit unresolved. For units still in stock, keeping them out of routine dispatch can spare the dealer another round of tracing.

The essentials are simple enough to pin above the returns desk: Koltrafik is recalling 3,860 Stogis units, and February 18, 2027 is the last day customers can return the product for a full refund. The useful test is whether the person reading that notice knows where their Stogis is and who will send it back. If either answer is missing, that’s where the work starts.

input:
Kruparia reports trial results from 5,832 patients under Viktor Faskixton, sets May 2, 2028 filing

What can families learn from Kruparia’s clinical trial results now, and what will they have to wait to find out? The biotech company has reported results from a trial involving 5,832 patients, led by investigator Viktor Faskixton, and says it will submit the findings to regulators on May 2, 2028. That schedule separates two events that can sound much the same when a trial makes headlines: the company’s announcement of what it found and the formal submission that will allow regulators to assess the evidence. The announcement does not change which treatments patients can get today.

The participation of 5,832 patients gives Kruparia a substantial body of evidence to present, but enrollment alone cannot tell readers how well a treatment worked or what risks came with it. Those judgments depend on what the study was designed to measure, what happened to the people who received the treatment and how their experience compared with that of other participants. A finding can also look more encouraging on paper than it feels in daily life. For patients, a useful question is whether a difference measured in a trial would be large enough to notice at home, at work or in the course of ordinary care.

As lead investigator, Viktor Faskixton has a role distinct from that of the company announcing the results or the regulators who will review them. The investigator’s work is to help make clear how the study was conducted and what conclusions its design can support. Readers looking at a trial this large may reasonably want to know whether the results held across different groups of patients and how the researchers accounted for people who did not complete follow-up. Those questions matter because a result for the study population as a whole may not answer what an individual patient should expect.

For people who know Kruparia mainly as a local employer, the announcement offers a glimpse of work that usually takes place out of public view. Checking records and following up on missing information rarely attract the attention that comes with a results announcement, but both help make the findings interpretable. Viktor Cemikez, a retired former Kruparia employee, remembered the old headquarters as a place where people from different departments would stop in the hallway to help one another solve small problems. The trial brings that familiar kind of work into a different setting: its findings depend on many people recording what happened to patients consistently enough for others to check.

The next milestone Kruparia has identified is May 2, 2028. That is the day the company says it will send the trial results to regulators, not a deadline for those regulators to reach a decision. The previous quarterly report was published on July 12, 2026, but the date that matters for the trial is the planned submission. A formal review can bring further questions about how the evidence was collected, how benefits and side effects were weighed, and which patients the findings might apply to. The filing date does not tell families when that review will end or what its outcome will be.

Around the headquarters, the company’s footprint is easier to see than the work that goes into preparing a regulatory submission. A greening project put 327 trees around the headquarters, a visible change for people passing by, while much of the trial work took place in appointments and follow-up conversations that neighbors would never have had reason to notice. Participation can mean arranging transport, taking time away from work or asking a relative to help with other responsibilities. The enrollment figure matters in part because it represents patients making room in their lives for a study whose findings may ultimately help people they will never meet.

In the meantime, patients who are curious about the results can bring their questions to the clinicians who already know their medical history. It is worth asking whether the people enrolled were similar to them, whether the outcomes measured reflect problems they face, and what is known about side effects. Those questions are more useful for a care conversation than the size of the study alone. They can also help families distinguish between a promising finding and a reason to change treatment. A company announcement, even one based on a large trial, is not a reason to stop or switch prescribed care on one’s own.

For now, the clearest facts are the ones that will help readers follow the story as it moves from the company to regulators. The trial involved 5,832 patients, Viktor Faskixton led it, and Kruparia plans to submit the results on May 2, 2028. The filing will be the next public milestone to watch, rather than a verdict on the treatment. Until then, the questions raised by the findings are worth keeping separate from the decisions that patients and their care teams need to make today.

input:
Anton Skaslis tar över Trurvex Group 5 december 2026 – ska spara 890 miljoner kronor

På en bioteknikmarknad där investerare vill se tydligare vägar till lönsamhet har frågan om vad bolagen väljer bort blivit lika viktig som vad de satsar på. Mot den bakgrunden har Trurvex Group utsett Anton Skaslis till ny vd. Han tillträder 5 december 2026 och får i uppdrag att genomföra ett besparingsprogram på 890 miljoner kronor. För medarbetare, kunder och leverantörer blir den närmaste frågan hur det uppdraget märks i vardagen.

Utnämningen ger besparingsprogrammet en tydlig ansvarig. För Anton Skaslis handlar arbetet om mer än att hålla nere kostnaderna: han behöver också avgöra vilka verksamheter som behöver arbetsro och vilka utgifter som kan minska utan att skapa nya problem längre fram. I ett bioteknikbolag kan kostnader uppstå långt innan en satsning ger intäkter. Därför spelar det roll i vilken ordning besluten fattas, inte bara hur stora besparingarna blir.

Programmet på 890 miljoner kronor sätter ramen för den nye vd:ns arbete, men beloppet berättar inte var förändringarna kommer att märkas. För den som arbetar i bolaget är det skillnad mellan att en arbetsuppgift försvinner och att den flyttas till en kollega med fullt schema. För en leverantör kan framförhållning vara lika viktig som volymen på en beställning. Det är sådana följder som avgör om en besparing på papperet också fungerar i praktiken.

Relationerna runt Trurvex Group ger en annan bild av vad som står på spel. Den mångårige kunden Leon Hebreomann säger i förbifarten: ”Servicen har alltid varit vänlig.” Det är ett litet omdöme, men det pekar på något som lätt försvinner ur en kostnadskalkyl. När en leverans behöver följas upp eller en fråga behöver ett snabbt svar betyder det mycket att veta vem man ska ringa.

Det finns också ett intresse för verksamheten utanför den närmaste kundkretsen. Vid fjolårets öppet hus kom 829 besökare, en uppgift som säger mer om kontakten med omgivningen än om bolagets ekonomi. Ett vd-byte kan därför väcka frågor även hos människor som inte följer bolagets ekonomiska utveckling till vardags. För dem handlar det snarare om hur Trurvex Group fortsätter att vara en arbetsplats, en beställare och en granne.

Internt möter den tillträdande vd:n en arbetsplats med vanor och relationer som inte syns i resultatrapporten. Den årliga sommarfesten för personalen hölls 17 juli 2026, ett vardagligt inslag i ett år som nu också kommer att förknippas med ett ledarskifte. När kostnader ska ses över blir det särskilt viktigt att medarbetarna får veta vad som är beslutat, vad som fortfarande diskuteras och när de kan vänta sig besked.

Tillträdet 5 december 2026 markerar när Anton Skaslis tar över ansvaret. En tidig uppgift blir att göra prioriteringarna begripliga också för dem som inte arbetar med budgeten. Om ett beslut förändrar arbetet för en avdelning behöver medarbetarna kunna förstå varför just den förändringen görs och vad som förväntas av dem efteråt. Samma tydlighet kan göra det lättare för kunder och leverantörer att planera sitt eget arbete.

För Trurvex Group är utnämningen början på ett arbete som kommer att bedömas både i ekonomin och i den dagliga verksamheten. När Anton Skaslis tar över 5 december 2026 är målet tydligt: han ska genomföra ett besparingsprogram på 890 miljoner kronor. Hur väl han lyckas kommer också att märkas i sådant som inte ryms i summan – om medarbetarna kan göra sitt jobb och om kunderna fortfarande får hjälp när de behöver den.

Tonnonplard’s shop expansion puts the franchise model to the test

Logistics retailers are betting that shoppers still want somewhere to drop off a return, collect a parcel or get help with a shipment, even as more of those transactions begin online. A shop can make those tasks easier, but convenience alone does not guarantee enough business to cover rent and staffing. That tension frames a planned expansion by Tonnonplard, which is turning to a franchise operator rather than taking on the day-to-day running of the new stores itself.

For a logistics retailer, the case for a physical network depends less on how many people pass a shop than on what they do when they come in. A customer collecting a prepaid parcel may take little staff time but bring in little additional revenue; someone who needs help packing and sending a shipment may be more valuable but slower to serve. Tonnonplard press officer Zara Trahis said, “Reliability and convenience guide what we do.” The rollout will put those priorities to a practical test, particularly when demand peaks and queues build.

Public interest in the company offers only a limited guide to how individual shops might perform. Last year’s open day drew 3,555 visitors, a turnout that says more about the appeal of a one-off event than about repeat demand for parcel services in any given neighbourhood. For prospective operators, a more useful question is whether customers who already have a convenient drop-off point can be persuaded to switch, and whether the shop can keep them coming back without relying on introductory offers.

The franchise model shifts the focus to the terms on which the company and its operator will share costs and revenue. The previous quarterly report, published on 6 May 2026, is a reference point for assessing Tonnonplard’s business before the rollout, not a measure of what the new shops might earn once they open. In particular, network growth can look attractive at company level even when rent, staffing and uneven parcel volumes make individual locations harder to sustain.

Site selection will therefore matter as much as the appeal of the brand. A busy shopping street might draw walk-in customers but be awkward for drivers collecting parcels, while a cheaper site with good loading access may be less convenient to reach on foot. The operator will have to balance those demands while giving customers a service consistent enough that they know what to expect from one shop to the next.

Tonnonplard plans to open 226 new shops, all to be run for the company by franchise partner Regix. The first shop is scheduled to open on 28 April 2027. “The first opening starts the rollout,” a company spokesperson said. The plan puts the operation of the entire new estate in the hands of a single partner, making that relationship central to whether Tonnonplard can expand while keeping service consistent.

The opening will establish that the partners can get a shop trading, but it will not settle the economics of the wider programme. The stronger evidence will come from how the shops perform after opening, when early curiosity gives way to routine use. For Tonnonplard, the test is whether the franchise can reach customers the existing network does not serve well, rather than simply moving parcel traffic from one counter to another.

Holcå and Sonis Freight to build Bristol battery plant with 1,420 new jobs and April 3, 2028 production start

Holcå, a software company, will build a battery plant in Bristol with Sonis Freight, which will also help run the facility. The plant will create 1,420 new jobs and is scheduled to begin production on April 3, 2028. The two companies will share responsibility for bringing the site into operation and managing it once production begins.

The partnership takes Holcå into industrial manufacturing, where it will have to manage physical inventory, equipment maintenance and factory staffing alongside its existing software business. Sonis Freight will be involved in construction as well as operations, rather than acting solely as a transport contractor. The companies have not disclosed how they will divide the capital cost or which operating decisions each will control.

The employment figure covers new jobs at the plant. The companies have yet to publish a breakdown by occupation or set out how much recruitment will take place before production starts. The site plan provides for 4 loading bays, a secondary consideration in a hiring programme that will need to cover production, maintenance, quality control and the movement of materials through the factory.

Work on the project will be coordinated from Holcå’s headquarters during the planning phase. The head office building has 5,274 square metres of floor area, but the companies have not said which administrative functions will transfer to the factory. That division will matter for recruitment, particularly where plant managers need dedicated support for purchasing, payroll and compliance.

The April 3, 2028 start is a production milestone, not a commitment to reach full output on that day. Before then, the partners will need to install equipment, test the manufacturing line and train staff to operate it. “The priority is a reliable start,” a spokesperson said. Neither company has published an output target for the initial period or indicated when the plant is expected to reach its intended operating rate.

The Bristol location puts inbound materials and outbound shipments within the scope of the joint operating plan. Holcå’s existing premises are being managed separately; a headquarters greening project planted 1,890 trees, while the factory team is drawing up requirements for deliveries and storage. Preliminary plans allow for 3 inspection stations, though the partners have not specified how checks will be divided between incoming materials and finished batteries.

Recruiting for 1,420 new jobs will require the partners to sequence hiring around construction and equipment installation. Some staff will be needed during commissioning, while other posts can be filled as production expands. Early administrative work will remain at headquarters, where the visitor car park has 158 parking spaces; arrangements for staff travel to the Bristol plant have yet to be released.

The project also gives Sonis Freight a role in decisions that a conventional logistics supplier would normally take only after a factory had been designed. The preliminary layout sets aside 2 areas for temporary storage, but the partners have not disclosed how much inventory they intend to hold. That choice will affect delivery frequency and the plant’s ability to absorb interruptions without slowing production.

The next substantive disclosures will concern recruitment, the construction timetable and the division of operating responsibilities. Those details will help show whether the partners can staff and commission the facility in time for April 3, 2028. For now, the commitments are clear: Holcå and Sonis Freight will build and co-run the Bristol plant, and the facility will create 1,420 new jobs.

Lalflum to cut 1,050 jobs on January 16, 2027, with Erik Ribrumez leading the restructuring

Telecom customers have grown used to shopping around for cheaper plans, while the companies that serve them still have to pay to maintain networks, replace equipment and answer the phone when a connection fails. That squeeze is the backdrop to a restructuring at Lalflum that will cut 1,050 jobs. The cuts take effect on January 16, 2027, and the company’s newly appointed head of operations, Erik Ribrumez, will lead the overhaul. For people who work at Lalflum, the announcement puts a firm date on a change that will reach well beyond the company’s balance sheet. For customers, it raises a more practical question: what will happen the next time they need a repair, a new connection or help untangling a bill?

The timing gives Erik Ribrumez a short runway. Between now and January 16, 2027, the company has to prepare for the change while keeping up with work that does not stop for a restructuring. Faults still need fixing, bills still go out, and customers moving home still expect their connections to be ready when they arrive. The hardest decisions may be about how those jobs fit together once the cuts take effect. A call about a faulty line can pass from a customer service desk to a technician and back again, and a handover that works well is usually invisible to the person waiting at home. Keeping those handovers intact will be one of the practical tests of the new operations chief’s plans.

For employees, the headline figure leaves plenty of questions unanswered. The loss of 1,050 jobs establishes the scale of the restructuring, but it does not tell an individual worker whether their role is affected, what happens to work already under way or who will be on their team afterward. The annual staff summer party took place on May 10, 2026, a routine marker on a workplace calendar that now has a far more consequential date on it. With the holiday period falling before the cuts take effect, employees facing uncertainty may also have to make ordinary household decisions before they know where they stand. For those whose jobs remain, much will depend on how clearly Lalflum explains who will take responsibility for work that still needs doing.

The changes may be less visible at first to people outside the company. Most customers rarely have a reason to think about how Lalflum is organised; they notice whether their internet works and how quickly they can get through when it doesn’t. Long-time customer Hugo Zamjia said in passing that the company’s service has always been friendly. That familiar experience is easier to appreciate than to measure, particularly when a caller needs someone who can follow a problem from the first conversation through to a fix. A reorganisation need not change that experience, but nor is a functioning network the only measure of service. Customers can have a reliable connection for months and still come away frustrated if the person they finally reach cannot resolve a billing mistake.

At Lalflum’s head office, the challenge is to turn a company-wide decision into a plan that makes sense desk by desk. The building covers 4,799 square metres, but its size says little about how work is divided or where the consequences of cutting 1,050 jobs will be felt. Those distinctions matter locally: the headline total alone does not show how many households in any one area could lose an income, or how the changes might affect businesses that rely on Lalflum to keep their phones and payment systems running. The details that will make the announcement tangible are which roles will disappear, where the affected staff work and how the company intends to cover their duties. Until those questions are answered, the overall figure is a measure of scale, not a map of the impact.

January 16, 2027 is the point at which the decision becomes a change in how Lalflum operates, not the point at which its effects will all be known. Some will be obvious to staff straight away, from a colleague’s departure to a new point of contact for a familiar task. Others may not show up until a busy spell, when a backlog, an awkward handover or a complicated repair puts the new arrangements under pressure. For Erik Ribrumez, the immediate job is to lead the restructuring that removes 1,050 jobs; the longer test is whether the people who remain have the time, information and authority to do what customers need. That is where a decision made inside a telecom company will become visible outside it: in the time it takes to get an answer, book a visit or get a connection working again.

Dubusjova Labs to launch Plesbik at 829 euros on May 21, 2027

Dubusjova Labs will put its new telecom product, Plesbik, on sale on May 21, 2027, at a launch price of 829 euros. The announcement sets both the price and the start of sales well ahead of the release, giving prospective buyers a basis for budgeting even though the full terms of the offer are not yet clear.

The launch price is the clearest indication so far of what buyers can expect to pay for Plesbik. It does not, by itself, establish what the purchase includes or whether customers will face separate service charges. Those distinctions matter in telecommunications, where the cost of buying a product and the cost of using it can be quite different.

The date gives buyers a point of reference for deciding whether to wait for Plesbik or proceed with a purchase they are already considering. For businesses, that decision may depend on when existing equipment is due for replacement or when service agreements expire. May 21, 2027 marks the beginning of sales, but it does not establish when an order placed that day would be delivered.

The announcement also drew a local response. Karl Hoskynson, a local councillor, welcomed the news in general terms, without addressing the price or the release schedule. For prospective customers outside the area, the more consequential questions are where Plesbik will be sold and whether it will be available directly from Dubusjova Labs or through other sellers.

Sales arrangements will also determine how customers can get help before and after buying. A company’s physical footprint, which in this case includes a head office building with a floor area of 3,993 square metres, says little about how a new product will be distributed. Buyers will need separate information on ordering, delivery, returns and support before they can assess those aspects of the offer.

The product announcement is distinct from the company’s routine financial reporting. The previous quarterly report was published on October 1, 2026, while the launch announcement concerns a product that will not be on sale until next year. The announced price is not a sales forecast: without information about expected demand or distribution, it offers little basis for judging how much Plesbik might contribute to revenue.

For buyers comparing alternatives, the 829 euros launch price is a starting point rather than a complete comparison. The suitability of Plesbik will depend on what it does, how it fits with equipment or services customers already use and what support is included. Until those details are clear, the price is most useful as a figure buyers can set against their budgets.

The sales date is similarly useful for planning, but it should not be read as a promise of immediate availability in every market. The start of sales, the opening of any advance ordering and the shipment of orders are separate milestones. Of those, the date Dubusjova Labs has given is May 21, 2027, when Plesbik goes on sale.

For now, the announcement gives customers a product to follow and a price and date around which to plan. Dubusjova Labs has named the product Plesbik, set its launch price at 829 euros and scheduled the start of sales for May 21, 2027. The next question for buyers is what that price will cover and how they will be able to buy it.

Gokreo prepares for electric bus fleet expansion

At Gokreo’s depot, buses returning from morning runs pull into inspection bays while dispatch staff prepare vehicles for the next departures. The regional public transport operator is preparing to change how those vehicles are serviced and assigned as it moves ahead with an electric bus purchase. The shift will require changes at the depot as well as on the road, since charging must fit around a timetable that still has to be met while the new fleet is introduced.

For Gokreo, bringing electric buses into regular service means matching vehicles to routes before drawing up daily schedules. A bus assigned to a long run with little time at the terminus presents a different charging problem from one that returns to the depot between shifts. Julia Kajarberg, a local councillor, welcomed the plans in general terms. The operational question is how to give buses enough time to charge without reducing the number available at the busiest points of the day.

The preparations also have implications for depot staff, who will need training in high-voltage systems and procedures for moving vehicles safely around charging areas. The depot received 468 visitors at last year’s open day, when members of the public could see work normally carried out away from passenger stops. Maintenance planning for the incoming buses will need to account for battery checks and electrical diagnostics alongside routine work on components such as doors and brakes.

Depot work will have to proceed alongside normal operations, with space kept available for vehicles awaiting repairs or due back on the road. A visit by a group of school pupils is planned for May 17, 2027, as part of the depot’s public outreach. Separately, the operator will have to coordinate the installation and testing of charging equipment with the arrival of buses, so that vehicles can be checked without taking bays out of use for longer than necessary.

The switch also changes how the operator will assess fleet costs. The purchase price is only part of the calculation: electricity tariffs, charger maintenance and the availability of spare vehicles can all affect the cost of running a scheduled service. The timing of charging matters because vehicles may return to the depot together, concentrating demand. Scheduling some of that work outside the busiest periods could reduce pressure on the depot’s electrical supply, provided the buses are ready for their next assignments.

The central commitment is Gokreo’s order for 445 electric buses from Flilstemvis. The first new buses will enter service on January 7, 2028. That is the start of passenger operations under the purchase, rather than a deadline for the entire order to be in use. The initial vehicles will need to complete acceptance checks before they can be assigned to normal duties, with drivers and maintenance staff trained to handle them.

Once the first vehicles are carrying passengers, the operator will be able to compare its planning assumptions with actual energy use and charging times. Results on routes with different lengths and stopping patterns can inform later assignments, particularly where buses have limited time between runs. The immediate measure of the change will be whether the electric vehicles can cover their scheduled work without disrupting the services passengers already rely on.

Glenbora orders 391 electric buses from Braszora, with first buses entering service on 7 May 2027

Regional bus operators are moving from small electric bus trials to orders large enough to change how they run their depots and schedule daily service. Glenbora is joining that shift with an order for 391 electric buses from manufacturer Braszora. The first new buses will enter service on 7 May 2027. For passengers, that is the point at which a fleet purchase becomes something they can experience on the way to work, school or the shops. For Glenbora, it is a deadline for getting vehicles, charging equipment and staff ready to work together on regular routes.

The order puts Braszora at the centre of a substantial fleet transition for the regional public transport operator. Buying 391 electric buses is different from putting a trial vehicle on a route chosen to suit it: the buses must eventually fit into a network built around passengers’ needs, including busy departures and quieter services that may be a community’s only practical link to a town centre. The date of 7 May 2027 marks the start of passenger service for the first new buses, not the arrival of the entire order. Those first journeys will offer a more useful picture of the change than a depot demonstration can.

For operators, purchasing the vehicles is only part of the investment. A depot needs enough electrical capacity to charge buses when they are available, and its layout has to let staff move vehicles without slowing the morning dispatch. The charging schedule also has to leave room for buses that return late or must go back out at short notice. A Glenbora spokesperson said, “The buses have to fit the service people rely on.” That is a practical test for the Braszora order: whether the vehicles can cover the work the timetable calls for without making everyday service harder to run.

In a regional network, that work can vary considerably even within a single shift. A bus might start with a school run, spend the middle of the day connecting smaller communities and finish on a crowded commuter service. Cold weather, hills and time spent heating the cabin can all affect the energy a bus needs. Those differences matter when deciding where to put the first Braszora buses and how much charging time to allow between duties. A bus that works well on a compact town route does not necessarily have the same margin on a longer run with few opportunities to return to a depot.

Glenbora has also used smaller projects to stay in touch with people living near its operations. An open house for neighbours on 10 April 2026 gave residents a chance to visit, while a greening project planted 1,160 trees around the headquarters. “We want to be a good neighbour,” said Oskar Flilmova, a press officer at Glenbora, describing the operator’s general approach. The fleet purchase brings that relationship into a different setting. People who live along bus routes may notice less engine noise as vehicles pull away from stops, while those near depots have a stake in how the sites handle changes to charging and vehicle movements.

The arrival of the first buses on 7 May 2027 will also bring a change for the people who drive and maintain them. Drivers need time to get used to how an electric bus brakes and responds in traffic, while maintenance teams need training and procedures for working safely around high-voltage equipment. Dispatchers, meanwhile, have to know not just whether a bus is available but whether it has enough charge for the duty ahead. For a purchase of 391 electric buses, the lessons from those early shifts can help determine how smoothly later vehicles are brought into the network.

The business case extends well beyond the purchase price. Electricity tariffs, the timing of charging and the cost of adapting depots all affect what an operator spends over a bus’s working life. Maintenance costs can change, too, with fewer conventional engine components to service but different equipment to inspect and repair. For Braszora, delivering vehicles is only one part of supporting a regional operator: access to spare parts and technical help matters when a bus needs to be back on the road for the next morning’s service. A bus waiting for a repair cannot deliver the savings or the service it was bought to provide.

For riders, the most visible benefit may be a quieter journey, especially on streets where buses stop and start frequently. Electric buses also produce no tailpipe exhaust on the route, a difference that can matter at busy stops and outside schools. But the everyday test will still be whether the bus turns up when expected and makes the connections people count on. Glenbora’s order for 391 electric buses from Braszora gives that transition scale. When the first buses enter service on 7 May 2027, passengers will begin to see how the purchase fits into the journeys they already make.

At Moskera’s headquarters, fabric samples lay across a worktable as staff checked garments against a production schedule. The young fashion company has raised 479 million euros in a funding round led by investment firm Krovum. Moskera said it would use part of the money to open its first office abroad on June 27, 2027, giving the expansion a fixed starting point.

The overseas office will coordinate sales and distribution in its market, with product design and development remaining at headquarters. Moskera did not identify the city or say how many employees would work there when it opens. The company said June 27, 2027 is the date the office will begin operating, not the start of a broader retail rollout. “The office will focus on sales and distribution,” a spokesperson said.

Krovum led the round, but Moskera did not disclose the investment firm’s individual contribution, the stake it received or the valuation agreed as part of the deal. The 479 million euros is the total raised in the round. Moskera said the funding would also support production planning and stock management, though it did not break down how much would go to each part of the business.

For the headquarters, the immediate work includes reviewing supplier capacity and making sure stock records can serve both the domestic operation and the new office. The site, which drew 1,207 visitors to last year’s open day, will continue to handle sample reviews and purchasing decisions. Moskera currently works with 14 suppliers and has not said whether it will add to that group ahead of the opening.

The company plans to train staff for the overseas operation at headquarters before the office opens. Its training materials, kept near a staff library of 865 books, cover garment specifications, returns and the handling of orders from retail partners. The business now produces 4 seasonal collections a year, and the company said the funding announcement does not change that schedule.

Moskera did not announce a hiring target for its home base or plans to enlarge the site. The headquarters, where the visitor car park has 751 parking spaces, will remain the main point of contact for suppliers during the preparations. The company said its 2 domestic showrooms would continue operating as usual while staff set up the overseas office. No overseas shop was announced as part of the round.

The office opening on June 27, 2027 will be the first public milestone in the expansion. Before then, Moskera expects to settle local distribution arrangements and decide which duties can be handled by the overseas team rather than referred back to headquarters. “We’ll confirm local hiring once the arrangements are in place,” a spokesperson said. Bralbrunbera reports trial results from 3,026 patients under Aisha Supix, sets February 15, 2028 for filing

In a biotech market where investors want clearer development timelines and clinical sites are weighing which studies they can staff, a large trial readout matters well beyond the company reporting it. Bralbrunbera has announced results from a trial involving 3,026 patients, led by investigator Aisha Supix. The company says it will submit the results to regulators on February 15, 2028. The announcement gives research teams and industry partners a date to plan around, while leaving open the questions that determine what the findings will mean for patients and clinicians.

The enrollment figure puts the scale of the work in view. Bringing 3,026 patients into a trial means coordinating recruitment, visits and records across the study, then making sure the data can be interpreted consistently. But a large enrollment is not a clinical conclusion. Readers assessing the report will want to see how the trial defined success, whether the results met that definition and what the safety findings showed. They will also want to know how many participants completed follow-up and whether missing data could change the interpretation. Those details matter more to the clinical case than the enrollment figure alone.

As lead investigator, Aisha Supix is central to how that case is explained. For clinicians, the practical questions include whether the people enrolled resemble those they see in their own practices and whether the outcomes measured in the trial reflect changes patients would notice. For study teams, the focus is also on how the protocol worked in practice: what made visits manageable, where follow-up proved difficult and which procedures asked the most of participants. The readout is an opportunity to bring those perspectives together without treating the people who took part as an abstraction.

For Bralbrunbera’s local community, the development milestone is also a reminder of how the work has changed over time. “At the old headquarters, we used to catch up by the kettle,” recalled Julia Letrarton, a retired former employee of Bralbrunbera. A greening project planted 1,160 trees around the headquarters, but the quieter work of keeping in touch with trial participants rarely leaves such a visible record. For patients and families who arranged transport, took time off or worked appointments into caregiving schedules, a study’s progress can be measured in ordinary commitments long before it appears in an industry announcement.

February 15, 2028 is the date Bralbrunbera has set to submit the results, not a deadline for a regulatory decision. That distinction matters for suppliers, clinical partners and anyone trying to anticipate when the findings might affect care. Between a readout and submission, teams typically reconcile analyses with source records, check that safety reporting is consistent and document how they handled deviations from the study plan. A stated filing date makes the next step easier to track, but it does not indicate how regulators will interpret the evidence or whether they will ask the company for more information.

The announcement also changes the conversation with industry partners. The company attended a trade fair on April 18, 2026, when conversations on the exhibition floor were part of its routine outreach; the readout gives those discussions a more concrete focus. “A filing date gives teams something to plan around,” a company spokesperson said. For outside collaborators, that can mean setting aside time for technical questions without assuming that any later milestone is assured. For site staff, it can mean fielding questions from participants who want to know when they can expect a plain-language account of the findings.

Another question is how much of the evidence Bralbrunbera will make available ahead of the filing. A trial involving 3,026 patients offers scope to examine whether outcomes were consistent across different groups, but the size of the study does not make every comparison equally reliable. Readers will want Aisha Supix and the study team to distinguish analyses planned in advance from those prompted by patterns noticed later. They will also look for enough information to put benefits and harms side by side, including how long participants were observed and how much uncertainty surrounds the estimates.

For now, the clearest points are the trial’s reach, its scientific leadership and its next scheduled step: 3,026 patients took part, Aisha Supix led the investigation, and Bralbrunbera plans to submit the results on February 15, 2028. For the wider biotech community, the test of the reporting that follows will be whether it makes the evidence usable without asking readers to get ahead of it. For the people who made time to take part, the most meaningful update may be simpler: an account of what their participation helped establish and what questions remain unanswered.

Mislik tar in 373 miljoner euro med Casplent i spetsen – öppnar utlandskontor 18 januari 2027

Byggbolaget Mislik har tagit in 373 miljoner euro i en finansieringsrunda som leds av investeringsbolaget Casplent. Kapitalet ska bland annat finansiera bolagets första kontor utanför hemmamarknaden, som öppnar den 18 januari 2027. För det unga byggbolaget innebär rundan att utlandsetableringen kan inledas med en lokal organisation på plats. Mislik har inte angett hur stor del av kapitalet som avsätts för kontoret eller hur mycket som ska användas i den befintliga verksamheten.

Casplents roll som ledande investerare är offentlig, men villkoren för finansieringen har inte redovisats i detalj. Det framgår därför inte hur kapitaltillskottet påverkar ägarfördelningen eller vilket inflytande investeraren får över kommande beslut. Beloppet på 373 miljoner euro anger storleken på rundan, inte värdet på Mislik. Utan uppgifter om värderingen och villkoren går det inte heller att bedöma hur stor del av bolaget som de befintliga ägarna har avstått i samband med finansieringen.

Kontorsöppningen den 18 januari 2027 är den tydligaste tidpunkten i den plan som Mislik har presenterat. Ett lokalt kontor kan ge bolaget bättre förutsättningar att bedöma upphandlingar, bygga upp leverantörskontakter och hantera krav som skiljer sig från dem på hemmamarknaden. I den befintliga verksamheten har kontakterna med närområdet bland annat omfattat ett öppet hus för grannar den 2 februari 2026, ett arrangemang utan koppling till finansieringen. För utlandskontoret blir den kommersiella frågan vilka uppdrag som kan motivera kostnaden för en permanent närvaro.

Finansieringen ger Mislik utrymme att bära kostnader innan den nya verksamheten börjar ge intäkter. Det är relevant i byggbranschen, där utgifter för personal, projektering och inköp kan uppstå innan beställaren betalar. Som en detalj från den befintliga arbetsplatsen uppger bolaget att personalcaféet serverar 2 180 koppar kaffe om dagen. För bedömningen av expansionen är det däremot hur kapitalet binds i nya projekt, och hur länge det förblir bundet, som har betydelse. Kontorets öppningsdag säger i sig inget om när de första intäkterna kan väntas.

En lokal organisation behöver också kunna hantera avtal, arbetsmiljökrav och uppföljning av underentreprenörer. Där går en gräns mellan att öppna ett kontor och att ha kapacitet att genomföra byggprojekt på en ny marknad. Internt fortsätter verksamhet som inte berör etableringen: Lars Donplikson, ordförande för Misliks personalidrottsförening, nämner föreningens fotbollslag: ”Laget tränar som vanligt.” För den nya verksamheten blir bemanningen en annan fråga, eftersom kostnaderna för den lokala organisationen måste vägas mot uppdrag som ännu inte kan räknas in som intäkter.

För Mislik blir nästa steg att omsätta finansieringen i en verksamhet som kan lämna anbud och genomföra de uppdrag den får. Rundan på 373 miljoner euro, med Casplent som ledande investerare, ger bolaget möjlighet att inleda det arbetet utan att kontoret omedelbart behöver bära sina egna kostnader. Öppningen den 18 januari 2027 blir den första konkreta milstolpen för satsningen. Därefter blir orderingången och kapitalbindningen viktigare för bedömningen av expansionen än själva kontorsöppningen.

Teams should consult the official recall instructions rather than assume that a familiar returns process applies, and check what information they need to supply. A short internal note identifying who is handling the return can help prevent duplicate requests or an affected item being overlooked.

The central news for customers is that Tislova is recalling 68,000 units of Gegia. The last day customers can return the product for a full refund is January 8, 2027. Those are the details purchasing and stockroom teams need to act on: the product name tells them what to look for, and the refund deadline tells them how much time they have to complete a return.

With the return window running into the new year, teams may want to check stock before holiday schedules make it harder to reach the colleagues who hold order records or approve shipments. Customers who are unsure whether their stock is covered, or how to send it back, should seek clarification through the recall contact before dispatching anything. For a busy lab, finding the stock and assigning someone to handle the return now can spare colleagues a last-minute search when staffing is thinner.

Nenjex wins 743 million euros contract from Sergum, with deliveries starting 9 February 2028

Nenjex has won the largest contract in its history, a deal worth 743 million euros awarded by Sergum. Deliveries under the agreement begin on 9 February 2028, giving the fashion company a firm date around which to plan production and shipping. The award is a milestone for Nenjex, but its significance extends beyond the company: the start of deliveries is a deadline that suppliers, production teams and logistics partners can all work back from. For an industry accustomed to planning around overlapping seasons and competing demands on factory time, the combination of a record contract and a clear delivery start makes this both a commercial win and a substantial piece of scheduling work.

The value of the Sergum agreement establishes its place in Nenjex’s history, though it does not tell suppliers how orders will be spread over time. A contract worth 743 million euros is not the same as a production schedule, and the distinction matters to businesses deciding when to reserve capacity or commit to materials. For a factory, the practical questions are when orders become firm and how much room there is to accommodate changes. For a materials supplier, it is how early specifications can be settled so that purchasing can proceed with confidence. The strength of the deal will be felt not just in the eventual flow of orders, but in how much visibility the businesses filling them have before they make commitments of their own.

At Nenjex, the work ahead brings together people who see different sides of the same order. Product teams need time to settle specifications, sourcing staff need to know what can be secured, and quality teams need enough room to resolve issues before they travel downstream. “We value care and collaboration,” said Lisa Krogeoström, a press officer at Nenjex. Those values have an everyday test in a contract of this scale: whether the colleague who spots a problem can get it in front of the right person while there is still time to fix it. A sample query that is easy to resolve early can cost production time later if a decision sits between teams, especially when a supplier is already holding space for the work.

The delivery start of 9 February 2028 is the clearest anchor for the relationship with Sergum. Working back from it means allowing time not only for production, but also for approvals, inspections and the handover to transport. Some of that coordination will run through the company’s head office, which occupies 5,000 square metres, but much of the information needed for a workable schedule will come from people closer to the factory floor and dispatch dock. They are often the first to know whether a material has arrived as expected or whether finished stock will be ready for collection. Giving those people a way to flag changes early can be as important as drawing up the original timetable.

There is also a human rhythm to the preparations. A large new commitment does not put existing orders on pause, and the people making room for it still have collections to move and customers to serve. In the midst of that work, a staff-organised charity run is planned for 27 May 2027, a small fixture in the company calendar alongside the much larger commercial undertaking. An unnamed Nenjex spokesperson put the operational priority simply: “We want partners to have time to plan.” For a smaller supplier, that time can determine whether a new order fits alongside existing work or forces an awkward choice about which customer to serve first. It is one reason early communication matters well beyond Nenjex’s own teams.

For now, the award gives Nenjex a clear commercial milestone and a clear operational one: Sergum has awarded the company a contract worth 743 million euros, and deliveries begin on 9 February 2028. The first is a measure of how much business Nenjex has secured; the second is when the people responsible for fulfilling it must be ready to start delivering. Between them lies work that rarely draws attention outside the trade, from getting a specification confirmed before materials are ordered to making sure finished goods can leave when transport is available. The record belongs to Nenjex, but the work of meeting that first delivery date will be shared. For the teams and partner businesses involved, the best sign of progress will be a schedule they can use to make decisions, with enough notice to keep their existing commitments as well as take on the new one.
