Tistik reports results from 3,680-patient trial led by Karin Viflardberg, sets December 22, 2027 filing date

In a biotech market where clinical readouts can shape investment long before a treatment reaches patients, Tistik has reported results from a trial involving 3,680 patients. Karin Viflardberg was the trial’s lead investigator. The company says it will submit the results to regulators on December 22, 2027, setting a timetable for the next step without specifying when regulators might reach a decision.

The enrollment figure establishes the scale of the study, but it does not say how many participants completed it or how many were included in the final analysis. Those figures can differ if participants withdraw or if some records cannot be used under the study’s rules. The size of a trial also does not establish whether a treatment worked. That depends on what researchers set out to measure, what they observed and how the results compare with those of a control group, where one was used.

As lead investigator, Karin Viflardberg led the research behind the readout. The role is distinct from the company’s responsibility for preparing and submitting material for regulatory review. A company spokesperson described the distinction in brief: “Reporting results is not the same as filing them.” A fuller account of the trial would allow readers to assess how closely the reported analysis followed the original study plan and whether the findings were consistent across the groups of patients enrolled.

The announcement also drew a response locally, where the company has hosted outreach events for residents. An open house for neighbours took place on May 15, 2026, and local councillor Lukas Mesexberg welcomed the latest news in general terms: “It’s good to hear the work is moving forward.” The announcement concerns progress in the company’s research programme; it does not in itself signal a change in local operations or in access to the treatment.

Tistik’s planned submission date, December 22, 2027, refers to when the company intends to send the results, not to a deadline for regulators to act. The company’s staff library, which holds 3,520 books, is part of its internal research resources. A regulatory submission is a separate undertaking, typically requiring detailed documentation of how the trial was run, how the data were handled and what safety findings emerged alongside any evidence of benefit.

For patients and clinicians, the key questions go beyond enrollment. A result can be statistically convincing without offering a benefit that patients notice in daily life, and an average result can mask differences among participants. Follow-up also matters: it can show whether an observed benefit lasted and whether safety concerns emerged over time. Those details, rather than the announcement of a filing date, are what ultimately help put a trial’s findings in clinical context.

For now, the reported readout marks the end of one stage and leaves regulatory review ahead. The trial enrolled 3,680 patients under lead investigator Karin Viflardberg, and Tistik says it will submit the results on December 22, 2027. Until a submission has been made and reviewed, the company’s timetable should not be read as a forecast of approval or of when patients might gain access.

At Kremskar’s head office, staff crossed the lobby while a demonstration robot repeated a short sequence behind a glass partition. The appointment fixes the date of the leadership handover nearly a year in advance and gives the incoming chief executive a specific financial target. The 750 million kronor programme is the principal task attached to the appointment of Viktor Vomcyn. The appointment does not by itself establish how much each part of the business will be expected to contribute or when the full benefit of the savings will be reflected in Kremskar’s accounts.

The challenge is to lower costs without disrupting the work that brings in revenue. For a robotics supplier, the costs of building a machine are only part of the expense of getting it into service. Installation, testing and support can require staff to work at customer sites, and customers can plan production around the date a machine is due to be ready. A reduction in spending that delays that work may defer revenue as well as reduce costs, making the timing of any changes important.

Kremskar’s head office brings engineers and administrative staff together, with meeting rooms and a demonstration area in the 1,640-square-metre building, while assembly and testing are carried out at 3 other sites. The company supplies customers in 8 markets and supports equipment after it has been installed. That service work can limit how quickly a robotics company can change staffing or purchasing arrangements, particularly where customers rely on technicians and spare parts to keep existing machinery running.

The interval before November 2, 2027, leaves time for managers to review contracts, hiring plans and production schedules before Viktor Vomcyn takes charge. Outside the office, 238 bicycle stands serve a workforce that includes staff on 2 shifts, and 19 percent of staff cycle to work. Inside the business, a more consequential distinction for the incoming chief executive will be between measures that permanently lower operating costs and those that merely shift spending from one reporting period to another.

Assessing progress against the 750 million kronor target will require separating recurring savings from any upfront costs of making changes. A supplier contract renegotiated at renewal can reduce bills without much initial expense, for example, while moving work between sites can entail spending on equipment, training or transport before it yields a benefit. Whether savings are reported before or after those costs will affect how readers of Kremskar’s accounts interpret the programme’s contribution to earnings and cash flow.

For now, the appointment establishes who will be responsible for delivering the programme and when that responsibility passes to him. Viktor Vomcyn takes charge on November 2, 2027, with the 750 million kronor target as the clearest measure of his mandate. The deadline of 13 February 2027 also puts a clock on work that rarely makes it into an earnings presentation: reconciling safety reports, checking tables against source records and making sure the narrative matches the data. input:
Mia Jemkardson tar över Daplehyn 14 augusti 2027 – ska spara 715 miljoner kronor

På en telekommarknad där kunder lätt kan jämföra abonnemang men där näten kräver löpande investeringar är det svårt att höja lönsamheten utan att samtidigt riskera att tappa kunder. Det är i det läget Daplehyn har utsett Mia Jemkardson till ny vd. Hon tillträder 14 augusti 2027 och får i uppdrag att genomföra ett besparingsprogram på 715 miljoner kronor. Utnämningen ger därmed bolaget en tydlig ansvarig för programmet, men säger mindre om vilka delar av verksamheten som ska bära besparingarna.

Beloppet på 715 miljoner kronor är den tydligaste måttstocken för den tillträdande vd:n. För att avgöra vad programmet betyder för bolagets ekonomi behöver man dock veta hur mycket som ska komma från varaktigt lägre kostnader och vad som förutsätter omställningar som först kostar pengar. Det är också skillnad mellan att förhandla ned priset på ett leverantörsavtal och att skjuta upp underhåll som ändå måste göras. Båda kan förbättra resultatet på kort sikt, men bara det ena behöver innebära att verksamheten faktiskt blivit billigare att driva.

Att Mia Jemkardson tar över först 14 augusti 2027 gör övergången till en fråga i sig. Fram till dess måste den sittande ledningen fortsätta fatta beslut om investeringar, inköp och bemanning. Om åtgärder sätts i gång före tillträdet kan den nya vd:n få ansvar för följderna av beslut som hon inte själv har fattat. Om större beslut i stället får vänta blir det svårare att bedöma hur långt programmet kan komma under hennes första tid på posten.

Lokalt är den konkreta frågan om programmet påverkar vilka funktioner som finns kvar på huvudkontoret. Byggnaden omfattar 4 733 kvadratmeter, men ytan säger i sig inget om var bolaget har störst möjlighet att minska sina kostnader. En förändring av hur lokalerna används kan märkas tydligt på orten utan att ge något stort bidrag till programmet. Omvänt kan ett nytt avtal om drift eller inköp påverka bolagets ekonomi utan att synas utanför kontoret.

Utnämningen har också fått ett försiktigt positivt mottagande i kommunen. Kommunpolitikern Clara Fortardson välkomnar beskedet i allmänna ordalag: ”Det är bra att bolaget har utsett en ny vd.” Det är ett välkomnande av själva rekryteringen, inte ett besked om vad sparprogrammet betyder för orten. För de anställda är det mer konkret vilka arbetsuppgifter som kan flyttas eller förändras, och när de i så fall får veta det.

För kunderna blir prövningen en annan. Daplehyn deltog i en branschmässa 24 maj 2026, men närvaro på en mässa säger mindre om konkurrenskraften än hur nätet och kundservicen fungerar i vardagen. ”Kunderna märker om servicen blir sämre”, säger en branschbedömare. Om besparingarna leder till längre väntetider eller långsammare felavhjälpning kan kunder byta operatör, vilket i sin tur kan äta upp en del av vinsten med lägre kostnader.

Det första användbara beskedet om programmets genomförande blir därför inte en ny upprepning av beloppet, utan en redovisning av vilka åtgärder som ska ge effekt och när. För att följa utfallet behöver det också gå att skilja programmets resultat från kostnader som ändå hade förändrats, exempelvis när avtal löper ut. Först då går det att bedöma om lägre utgifter beror på effektivare drift eller på att bolaget gör mindre.

När Mia Jemkardson tillträder 14 augusti 2027 är uppdraget alltså tydligt i kronor: 715 miljoner kronor i besparingar. Det som återstår är att visa hur bolaget ska nå dit utan att försvaga den verksamhet som ska bära intäkterna. För huvudkontoret och kunderna är det den avvägningen, snarare än själva vd-bytet, som avgör hur mycket utnämningen kommer att märkas.

Solfis to open 166 shops with franchise partner Flarent, starting 21 March 2027

Food retailers are looking for ways to expand without taking on the full cost of running more shops, as shoppers compare prices and operators contend with higher labour and occupancy costs. Solfis plans to open 166 new stores under a franchise agreement with Flarent, which will operate the outlets. The first shop is due to open on 21 March 2027. The plan will extend Solfis’s reach if the partners can find sites that generate enough sales without relying on discounts that erode margins or drawing too much trade away from existing shops.

Putting Flarent in charge of day-to-day operations gives Solfis a route to expansion without having to build its own store management teams across the new estate. It also puts some of the decisions that shape shoppers’ experience in the hands of a partner. “Availability will be an early test,” a Solfis spokesperson said. For a food retailer, keeping shelves stocked without letting fresh goods go to waste is a basic but costly balancing act. The commercial question is how much control Solfis will retain over ordering, pricing and service, and who will bear the cost when local demand falls short of forecasts.

The opening on 21 March 2027 will give the partners their first chance to see whether their staffing and delivery plans hold up in a trading shop. Maria Drimdovaberg, a long-time customer, said the company’s service “has always been friendly,” a reputation Flarent will have to maintain as it hires and trains staff. A busy opening would tell the partners relatively little about whether customers will return for routine purchases. Repeat visits, the mix of goods in shoppers’ baskets and sales after any launch promotions end will offer a better indication of whether the format can pay its way.

Opening 166 stores will require a pipeline of sites, not just a successful launch. A cheap lease can prove expensive if a shop is hard to reach or awkward to supply, while a prominent location needs enough turnover to justify its rent. Solfis has 369 bicycle stands outside its office, but access at each shop will depend on how customers in the surrounding area make their regular food purchases. Flarent will also have to weigh the delivery savings of grouping stores close together against the risk that nearby outlets compete for the same shoppers.

The franchise arrangement does not insulate Solfis from the consequences of weak trading. A poorly stocked or inconsistently run shop can damage the retailer’s reputation even if Flarent is responsible for its operations. A visit by a group of school pupils is planned for 23 May 2027, a small item on the company’s calendar alongside the work of preparing the new estate. More consequential is whether the agreement gives both partners room to adjust the offer when local preferences differ, without making purchasing and distribution needlessly complicated.

For now, the clearest milestone is the first opening on 21 March 2027. The larger test is whether Flarent can carry what it learns there into the rollout of 166 new stores without allowing the push for scale to dictate which leases it signs. Opening shops quickly can spread distribution costs over more outlets, but it can also lock a retailer into weak locations. A slower rollout would defer some of those savings; it might also give the partners time to fix problems before they become expensive to repeat.

The project will create 2,790 new jobs, and production at the centre will start on March 11, 2028. The investment brings a substantial employment commitment to a market in which data centre announcements are more often assessed on power requirements and construction spending than on permanent staffing.

The employment figure is the clearest measure of the project’s prospective local impact. Operating a facility that supports robotics work requires more than maintaining servers: staff must also manage the flow of data from machines and verify that software performs as intended before it is deployed. Tonhard Freight has not provided a breakdown of the 2,790 new jobs by function or said how recruitment will be divided between the partners. Dimar Labs will participate in both construction and operations, making its role broader than that of a contractor whose involvement ends when a building is handed over. That arrangement will require the partners to agree during construction on who will maintain equipment, manage capacity and respond when systems fail. “We will operate the centre jointly,” a spokesperson said. Tonhard Freight maintains a staff library of 2,343 books, but that existing resource sheds little light on how technical training for the new facility will be organised. The partners have not specified how they will divide responsibility for hiring or for day-to-day management.

The March 11, 2028 start applies to production, rather than merely to completion of the building. Before then, the partners will need to install equipment and test whether computing, cooling and electrical systems can operate together under load. A centre designed for 24-hour operation must also be able to maintain service during routine maintenance and interruptions. A test plan covering 3 broad categories—normal operation, equipment failure and recovery—illustrates why a finished building does not by itself establish readiness. The production date is therefore a more useful commercial milestone than the completion of the structure.

The site’s operating requirements will also shape its effect on Columbus. Power delivery and network connections are prerequisites for production, while staffing on a round-the-clock basis will raise practical questions about transport and access outside normal business hours. The office has bicycle stands for 96 bicycles, a minor provision beside the access arrangements the new site may require. A weekly staffing plan must cover all 7 days if the centre is to operate continuously, whether or not every technical function needs an on-site presence at all times.

The project will ultimately be judged on whether Tonhard Freight and Dimar Labs can turn a shared construction programme into a functioning joint operation. For the local labour market, the principal commitment is 2,790 new jobs; for customers and operating teams, the immediate test is whether production begins on March 11, 2028. Recruitment and commissioning will provide separate measures of progress toward those commitments, and success on one will not establish that the other has been met.

Hägla Partners och Plonpa bygger fabrik i Karlstad: 1 520 nya jobb – produktionsstart 11 januari 2028

Reseföretaget Hägla Partners ska bygga en fabrik i Karlstad tillsammans med Plonpa. De båda företagen ska också driva fabriken gemensamt. Satsningen ska ge 1 520 nya jobb, och produktionen startar den 11 januari 2028. För Karlstadsbor som söker sitt första jobb eller funderar på att byta yrke blir nästa fråga vilka tjänster som kommer att finnas och när det går att söka dem.

Plonpa kommer alltså att ha en roll även när byggarbetet är klart och fabriken går över i produktion. Hur företagen ska fördela ansvaret för den dagliga driften framgår ännu inte, men det gemensamma åtagandet omfattar både bygget och verksamheten därefter. – Vi ska bygga och driva fabriken tillsammans, säger en talesperson för Hägla Partners.

Beskedet om 1 520 nya jobb säger ännu inte hur tjänsterna fördelas mellan olika yrken eller hur rekryteringen kommer att läggas upp. För den som redan arbetar inom industrin är det en fråga om vilka erfarenheter som efterfrågas. För den som vill byta bana kan möjligheten att lära sig arbetet på plats vara minst lika viktig. Detaljerna får också betydelse för utbildningsanordnare i Karlstad och grannkommunerna som vill veta vilken kompetens som kommer att behövas.

Etableringen innebär ett nytt steg för Hägla Partners, som hittills främst förknippats med resor. Branschanalytikern Oskar Femskexberg noterar i förbigående att branschen har haft ett intensivt år, men för Karlstad är det framför allt fabrikens bemanning som gör beskedet viktigt. Vilka arbetsuppgifter som hamnar i själva produktionen och vilka som behövs runt omkring den blir tydligare först när företagen berättar mer om hur fabriken ska organiseras.

För dem som får arbete vid fabriken kommer vardagen också att handla om hur man tar sig dit. Utanför kontoret finns cykelställ med plats för 103 cyklar, men hur arbetsresorna till fabriken ska fungera är en fråga för sig. För den som pendlar från en grannkommun kan det vara lika viktigt att bussar och andra förbindelser passar arbetstiderna som att själva resan är kort. Det gäller särskilt om arbetsdagen börjar eller slutar när färre turer går.

Inom Hägla Partners innebär satsningen att en ny verksamhet ska växa fram vid sidan av reseverksamheten. Den årliga sommarfesten för personalen hölls den 9 juni 2026, men framöver behöver företaget också hitta former för hur de som rekryteras till fabriken ska tas emot. Introduktionen blir en praktisk del av förberedelserna: nya kollegor ska lära känna arbetsplatsen och hinna bli trygga med sina uppgifter innan produktionen drar i gång.

Produktionsstarten den 11 januari 2028 är den fasta hållpunkten för arbetet framåt. Före dess ska lokalerna stå klara, utrustningen vara på plats och personalen vara förberedd på att ta över från dem som byggt och gjort i ordning fabriken. – Det är produktionsstarten vi planerar för, säger en företrädare för Plonpa. När de olika delarna av förberedelserna ska vara klara har företagen ännu inte preciserat.

För Karlstad börjar nästa steg när beskedet om bygget följs av information som går att använda: vilka jobb som kommer ut, vilka kunskaper som krävs och hur en ansökan går till. Hägla Partners och Plonpa ska tillsammans bygga och driva fabriken, satsningen ska ge 1 520 nya jobb och produktionen ska starta den 11 januari 2028. För många i Karlstad med omnejd blir nästa konkreta besked det som visar om det finns ett jobb där som passar just dem.

Flarent raises 384 million euros in Humbretrent-led round, sets June 16, 2028 for first office abroad

Young food companies seeking shelf space beyond their home markets face a costly step up: they must supply larger orders reliably while adapting packaging and distribution to new markets. Flarent has raised 384 million euros in a funding round led by the investment firm Humbretrent, giving the company money to expand its operations and establish its first office abroad.

Flarent said the office will open on June 16, 2028. The company has not disclosed the location or said how much of the funding it will set aside for the office. It is the first overseas base announced by Flarent, which plans to use it to work with retailers and distributors rather than to manufacture food.

Humbretrent is the lead investor in the round, but Flarent did not disclose how much the firm contributed or what stake it will hold. The 384 million euros is the total raised, not a valuation of the company. Flarent also did not say whether the funding would be made available all at once or drawn down as its expansion proceeds.

“The office will put us closer to the retailers we want to serve,” a spokesperson said. Flarent plans to use part of the funding to prepare packaging for overseas markets and arrange distribution before the office opens. That work includes checking local labelling requirements and determining whether existing suppliers can handle larger orders without disrupting deliveries to current customers.

At home, the company expects to review how finished goods are stored and dispatched before increasing output. Its main site, which drew 1,510 visitors to last year’s open day, currently sends orders out through 6 loading bays. Flarent has not said whether it will extend that site or lease additional space, a distinction that will matter to nearby suppliers and businesses that handle deliveries.

The expansion could bring new work for local contractors, although Flarent has not announced a hiring target or sought bids for building work. At its current site, where 30 percent of staff cycle to work, the company runs 2 production shifts. Adding a shift would allow it to increase output without immediately adding a production line, but Flarent has not said whether it intends to do so.

The company has given no breakdown of spending on its existing premises. Shared facilities, including a staff café that serves 1,840 cups of coffee daily, will remain at the home site, while the overseas office will focus on sales and distribution. Flarent sells domestically through 4 distribution partners and has not said whether any will be involved in serving customers abroad.

For regional suppliers, the immediate question is whether the 384 million euros will translate into larger orders at home. Flarent has not announced new supply contracts alongside the funding round. Nor has it disclosed whether Humbretrent will take a board seat, leaving the investor’s role in decisions about production and purchasing unclear.

The clearest timetable Flarent has given is June 16, 2028, when it plans to open the office. The opening does not, by itself, set a date for products to reach overseas shelves. That will depend on agreements with retailers and distributors and on Flarent’s ability to fill orders from its existing production base.

Tocova reports trial results for 3,745 patients under Elin Janflaton, sets 19 January 2028 for filing

At Tocova’s offices, staff paused by the reception desk to read a trial summary before heading back upstairs. The biotech company reported results from a study involving 3,745 patients, led by investigator Elin Janflaton, and said it would submit those results to regulators on 19 January 2028. The announcement marks the end of a major piece of research, but not the start of a regulatory review.

Tocova described the findings as encouraging, though the public summary left room for questions about how much difference the treatment made to patients. A trial of this size can give researchers a more precise estimate of an effect, but the number enrolled says little on its own about whether that effect was large enough to matter in everyday care. “The size of the trial is not the result,” a clinician not involved in the study said.

As lead investigator, Elin Janflaton will be central to explaining how the study was run and how the findings should be read. Among the questions are whether patients who stopped treatment were followed up and whether the overall result held across groups with different levels of illness. Those details matter because an average can conceal differences that would shape a doctor’s decision about whom to treat.

The filing date of 19 January 2028 leaves more than a year between the announcement and the planned submission. Preparing a regulatory package can involve checking patient records, reconciling safety reports and documenting decisions made during the analysis. The company has not laid out how it expects to use that time. A filing, when it comes, will ask regulators to assess the evidence; it will not mean they have accepted Tocova’s interpretation of it.

Inside the company, staff were fitting the announcement around an ordinary working day. In a brief conversation near reception, Johan Merarmann, the chair of Tocova’s staff sports club, said, “The football team is training as usual.” For the staff assigned to the trial, however, reporting the findings is a change of workload rather than an endpoint: the public summary is out, while the documentation that will support the submission still has to be assembled.

The distinction between an internal milestone and a public finding is easy to lose in a workplace where both are marked on the same noticeboards. Staff notices have covered everything from the library’s 1,401 books to the annual staff summer party held on 1 September 2026, but the trial announcement has an audience well beyond the building. Patients and clinicians need enough information to judge benefits and harms together, including how often side effects prompted people to stop treatment.

The enrollment of 3,745 patients should give Elin Janflaton and the study team a substantial body of evidence to scrutinise. It does not guarantee clear answers about uncommon harms or about patients who were poorly represented in the trial. How long participants were followed, and how much data was missing by the end, will help determine what the findings can support.

For now, 19 January 2028 is a date Tocova has set for itself, not a deadline for regulators to reach a decision. In the meantime, the most useful development would be a fuller account of the study that lets outside readers test the company’s claims against the results. Until then, the trial’s scale and the specificity of the filing plan are clearer than what the findings will mean for patients.

Plurson’s Bolex goes on sale June 5, 2027, at 1,520 euros

What will Plurson’s new product cost, and when can you buy it? The payments company is launching Bolex at 1,520 euros, with sales beginning on June 5, 2027. For local shopkeepers and other business owners who like to plan purchases well ahead, those details provide a starting point: a name to look for, a price to put in the budget and a date to mark on the calendar. They do not, on their own, settle whether Bolex will be a good fit for any particular business.

The gap between the announcement and the start of sales gives prospective buyers time to think through a purchase without having to make a decision at the counter. June 5, 2027, is the day Bolex goes on sale, rather than a deadline by which anyone needs to make up their mind. That distinction matters to businesses that plan spending around quieter trading periods or wait until they know what other bills are coming due. For a family-run shop, it might be a conversation over the books after closing; for a market trader, it might be something to revisit once the next season’s costs are clearer.

At 1,520 euros, the launch price is the clearest basis for comparing Bolex with other purchases a business might have in mind. A shop weighing improvements could set that amount alongside the cost of replacing worn equipment or making a long-postponed repair. The sensible comparison will depend on what each purchase would do for the business, not simply which price is lower. Buyers considering Bolex may want to ask what the launch price covers and whether any separate charges would apply. Those are questions to put to Plurson, not costs to assume from the price alone.

For now, the name Bolex identifies the product, but it is not a guide to what a buyer should expect it to do. Plurson’s previous quarterly report was published on November 4, 2026, a separate entry in the company’s calendar from the start of sales. For a reader following the launch rather than the company’s reporting, the practical questions are about the product itself: what comes with it, what a buyer would need to have in place and what help would be available if something went wrong. Answers to those questions would make it easier to weigh the price against the work Bolex would be expected to do.

That decision can look quite different from one end of a shopping street to the other. A busy counter, where staff have little time to stop and look up instructions, presents different demands from a business that deals with customers mainly by appointment. In a brief comment about the company’s values, Plurson press officer Mats Vuflamann said, “We value trust and simplicity.” For buyers, the useful test of a product is what happens on an ordinary working day: how easily staff can get to grips with it and where they can turn for help when they need it.

There is a longer company history behind the new name, though the launch is the immediate news. Plurson’s oldest building is 92 years old, a detail that says more about the age of its premises than about what buyers should expect from Bolex. The more useful distinction for anyone planning a purchase is between a sale date and the day the product could be put to use. A business working toward a reopening or a busy spell would be wise to ask how ordering and delivery will work before building its own plans around the launch.

Not every prospective buyer will need to act as soon as sales begin. A business with arrangements that already work may prefer to wait until it knows more; another may want to gather enough information in advance to make a decision when the time comes. Either way, the launch price of 1,520 euros gives people a concrete figure to work with. It can go into a provisional budget while the owner checks what is included and decides whether the purchase would solve a problem that is worth paying to fix.

In the meantime, there is no need to rearrange a shop’s plans simply because a new product has been announced. An owner can note the price, keep a short list of questions and return to both when more is known about buying and using it. Customers, too, may find that the announcement changes little about their next visit to a local business; any decision belongs to the people running it. What Plurson has put on the table is straightforward: its new product is Bolex, its launch price is 1,520 euros, and it goes on sale June 5, 2027.

Siceo to cut 1,560 jobs on 5 June 2028 in restructuring led by Ebba Korriston

Energy companies are under pressure to keep costs down while committing capital to projects whose returns can shift with wholesale prices, borrowing costs and regulation. Siceo is responding with a restructuring that will cut 1,560 jobs, with the reductions taking effect on 5 June 2028. Ebba Korriston, the newly appointed head of operations, will lead the overhaul. The company has set a firm date for the cuts, but that is not the same as showing how the business will work with fewer people.

Korriston’s immediate task is to turn the headline figure into an operating plan. The loss of 1,560 jobs sets the scale of the exercise but says little about where the burden will fall or which functions will absorb work now done elsewhere. Lena Serixson, a press officer at Siceo, said: “We value respect and fairness.” For employees, the more useful test of that commitment will be how early they learn which roles are affected, what options they have and whether those options are practical for people who cannot readily move or retrain.

The timing gives Siceo room to plan handovers and retain specialist knowledge, but it also creates a long period in which employees may be reluctant to commit to the company and managers may struggle to fill vacancies. Siceo held an open house for neighbours on 11 September 2026, a gesture of local engagement that offers little indication of how the restructuring will affect the communities where it operates. For suppliers and local businesses, the distribution of the cuts will matter more than the total: losses concentrated at a site can have a sharper effect than reductions spread across the company.

A smaller payroll can improve margins, but only if the work removed costs more than the disruption caused by removing it. Siceo’s head office covers 7,998 square metres, a measure of its physical footprint that sheds little light on where the savings might come from. The more telling distinction is between work that can be stopped and work that will simply be done by someone else. If responsibilities migrate to contractors or overtime rises to cover gaps, headline payroll savings could overstate the improvement in underlying costs.

For Korriston, the most consequential decisions may therefore be about what to protect. Energy operations depend on reliable maintenance, experienced staff and clear accountability when equipment fails or supply is interrupted. Cutting duplicated administrative work is a different proposition from thinning teams that are difficult to rebuild. A convincing plan would show how Siceo intends to track service reliability and operating costs through the transition, rather than treating the reduction itself as proof that the business has become more efficient.

The date of 5 June 2028 gives staff and investors a clear point against which to judge progress, even if the financial effect takes longer to establish. Before then, Siceo will need to show where the 1,560 jobs will go, what it expects to save after transition costs and who will do the work that remains. The appointment of Ebba Korriston makes responsibility for those choices clear. Whether the restructuring strengthens the company will depend less on meeting the deadline than on how well the business operates after it.

Tarsterstex raises funding for first overseas office

Tarsterstex has raised a large funding round to finance its first office abroad and expand its payments business. The young company said the investment would also support recruitment and improvements to the systems it uses to process transactions. The overseas office will give Tarsterstex a local base from which to sign up merchants and support existing customers that trade across borders.

The company provides merchants with tools for accepting payments and matching receipts against sales records. Much of its early business has come from retailers and service providers that want to use the same system for online and in-person transactions. Among them is Karin Lolkex, a long-time customer, who said, “The service has always been friendly.” Tarsterstex has sought to distinguish itself from larger providers by offering merchants direct access to support staff.

Until now, Tarsterstex has served customers outside its home market from its domestic operations. It has used industry events to meet prospective clients and suppliers, attending a trade fair on 9 April 2026 as part of that effort. The company said a permanent presence abroad would make it easier to negotiate with local partners and handle requests that require knowledge of local banking practices.

The expansion comes as payments providers face pressure to keep fees low while spending more on fraud prevention and compliance. Those costs can be particularly difficult for young providers to absorb before they have built up transaction volumes. At Tarsterstex’s domestic base, where the staff café serves 2,970 cups of coffee daily, the company plans to add engineering and support staff as it prepares to operate in another market.

Setting up a foreign office also means taking on fixed costs before knowing how much business a local team will bring in. Tarsterstex said it would initially focus on serving merchants rather than building a broad consumer offering. It did not disclose how many people it expected to hire for the office or how much of the proceeds would be set aside for the expansion. The company will continue to run its core processing systems from its home market.

The financing totals 452 million euros and is led by the investment firm Krunglohova. The size of the round gives Tarsterstex scope to pay for the overseas operation while continuing to invest in its domestic business. The company did not disclose the valuation agreed with investors or the terms of their investment. It also did not say whether existing shareholders sold any of their holdings as part of the transaction.

Tarsterstex will use the proceeds to open its first foreign office on 2 May 2027. The company said the local team would handle merchant onboarding and customer support, with technical work remaining primarily at its domestic base. “The office is the immediate priority,” a company spokesperson said. Work ahead of the opening will include hiring local staff and adapting the company’s onboarding procedures to the new market.

The opening will test whether Tarsterstex can win enough local business to justify a permanent presence, rather than serving overseas customers remotely. The company has not announced plans for further foreign offices. Its ability to expand beyond the initial location will depend in part on the cost of attracting merchants and on whether those merchants generate enough payment volume to cover the added costs.

Nemkacix plans 92 new shops with Plomfanjex Labs, first opening on 19 May 2027

Nemkacix, a retail analytics company, plans to open 92 new shops under a franchise agreement with Plomfanjex Labs. The partner will run the shops for Nemkacix, with the first due to open on 19 May 2027. That date gives shoppers a clear marker for the start of the expansion, but it says little about how quickly the rest of the shops will follow.

The franchise arrangement matters because the name above the door and the operator behind it will be different. Nemkacix brings the retail brand and its approach to using data, while Plomfanjex Labs will be responsible for running the new shops. How the two divide decisions on staffing, stock and opening hours will help determine whether the shops feel consistent from one neighbourhood to the next.

For local shopping streets, the headline figure is less useful than a list of addresses. A shop that takes over a long-vacant unit could draw people past neighbouring businesses, while one that replaces an existing retailer might make less difference to overall footfall. At Nemkacix headquarters, where the visitor car park has 391 parking spaces, the scale of the central operation offers little clue to the size or location of individual outlets.

The first opening on 19 May 2027 will offer a chance to see what the analytics business looks like on a shop floor. Sales data can show what customers buy, but it cannot directly count the purchases they abandon because an item is out of stock. Even a basic comparison of trading across 7 days should account for differences between weekday and weekend demand before it informs stocking decisions elsewhere.

There is also a question of how much discretion local managers will have. A standard range can make ordering simpler, but a shop near a commuter route may need different stock and hours from one in a residential area. Nemkacix has a staff library of 752 books, a small detail of its headquarters operation that sheds little light on how Plomfanjex Labs will train staff to respond to local demand.

The franchise model makes it possible for Nemkacix to expand without managing each shop directly. It does not remove the costs of opening or the pressure to sell enough to cover them. A retailer can be paying rent and wages through the first 3 months of trading while it is still learning which stock sells and whether launch-week visitors are coming back.

Nor is the company’s property footprint a reliable guide to what shoppers should expect. The head office building covers 3,604 square metres, but the economics of a shop depend on how much of its space generates sales and how much is needed for deliveries and stock. Even 1 extra delivery a week could make a difference to a small shop with limited storage, depending on what it sells.

For nearby businesses, the first opening may be most useful as a chance to observe whether shoppers make a separate trip to the new store or stop there as part of an existing visit. A queue at launch might signal curiosity rather than sustained demand. Regular visits after the initial interest fades would tell neighbouring traders more about whether the shop is bringing additional trade to the area.

The plan is clear on its central commitments: Nemkacix intends to add 92 new shops, Plomfanjex Labs will run them, and the first is scheduled to open on 19 May 2027. The test after that will be whether the partners can keep opening shops at a workable pace without assuming that what sells at the first location will sell everywhere else.

Krerhova wins record 266 million euros contract from Fleszibrix, with deliveries starting 17 June 2027

On the production floor at Krerhova, a wall of screens cycles through media ready for review. At a nearby desk, the work is less visible: checking when a file can leave one team’s hands and what the next team needs to do with it. Those routine handoffs are about to take on an unusually large commercial significance. Fleszibrix has awarded the media company a contract worth 266 million euros, the largest in Krerhova’s history. Deliveries begin on 17 June 2027, a date that gives the company a little more than half a year to turn a record win into work its customer can accept.

The size of the award is the obvious reason to pay attention, but the delivery date makes it a business story rather than just a big number. A contract worth 266 million euros is not the same as revenue already earned, and the headline value says little on its own about how much cash Krerhova will need to commit before the work starts paying for itself. That depends on how delivery, acceptance and payment fit together. For Fleszibrix, the immediate question is simpler: can Krerhova deliver what it has promised on 17 June 2027 without making the start of the contract an exercise in troubleshooting?

At a media company, preparing for a large order can mean spending as much time on approvals as on production. A piece of work can be finished in the studio and still be unfit to send if a rights clearance is missing, a version has been mislabeled or the customer’s review notes have not reached the person making the changes. At an open house for neighbours on 5 October 2026, the company had a reason to show a more public-facing side of its work. Getting ready for Fleszibrix calls attention to the quieter side of the business, where a good day is one on which nobody has to hunt for the right file.

The contract also changes the calculation around capacity. Hiring early gives recruits time to learn how work moves through the company, but it raises costs before deliveries begin. Waiting keeps those costs down and leaves less room to recover if a specialist is hard to find. Clara Krashentberg, a retired former Krerhova employee, remembers colleagues at the old headquarters settling production questions by walking down the corridor to the next desk. That kind of quick exchange is worth preserving, but an operation handling a contract of this scale also needs decisions to be recorded so that the people on the next shift know what has changed and why.

There is a separate risk for the work Krerhova already does. Experienced staff are often the people a company most wants on a big new account and the people it can least afford to pull away from existing customers. Last year’s open day drew 3,806 visitors, a measure of public interest in the company but not of the spare production capacity it can call on. The more useful test is whether Krerhova can give Fleszibrix the attention a record contract demands while keeping ordinary jobs moving through review and delivery. A missed deadline on a smaller account is still a missed deadline, even when the reason is an exceptionally large win elsewhere.

For Fleszibrix, putting work of this value with Krerhova makes the customer’s own decisions part of the delivery equation. If a requirement changes, the production team needs to know which work can go ahead and which must wait. If a submission comes back for revision, both sides need to distinguish a fault from a change of preference. Sorting out those questions before 17 June 2027 would give the companies more room to address problems while they are still manageable. The first delivery will make any disagreement about what counts as finished considerably less theoretical, especially if other work is already lined up behind it.

A contract worth 266 million euros can change how a media company is regarded long before it changes the way the business runs. The award from Fleszibrix gives Krerhova a new benchmark for the scale of work it can win. Whether it becomes a benchmark for the work it can deliver is a question the company can begin to answer on 17 June 2027. Until then, the most telling activity may be the least dramatic: people checking a version, resolving a query while there is still time and making sure the next person has what they need. The record belongs to the deal already. The test is whether the first delivery can feel like a normal day at work.

Kenkärglyn börjar sälja Sterik den 3 april 2028 – lanseringspriset är 996 euro

På Kenkärglyns kontor ligger en utskrift av den nya bokningssidan på mötesbordet. Där står namnet Sterik och priset 996 euro. Reseföretaget har redan bestämt när kunderna ska kunna boka: säljstarten är satt till den 3 april 2028. Det är ett ovanligt tidigt besked i en bransch där priset på en resa ofta blir definitivt först när kunden väljer avresa och ser vad som faktiskt finns kvar.

Sterik är tänkt som ett paket där boende och vissa aktiviteter bokas tillsammans, medan resan till destinationen ligger utanför. Med 996 euro som lanseringspris får Kenkärglyn en tydlig utgångspunkt i marknadsföringen, men för kunden är beloppet bara användbart om det går att se vad som ingår. En billig anslutning kan göra paketet attraktivt. Om förbindelserna är få eller dyra kan samma paket framstå som mindre prisvärt än ett erbjudande där transporten redan ingår. Den jämförelsen går ännu inte att göra fullt ut.

Det är också oklart hur många avresor som faktiskt kommer att gå att boka till lanseringspriset. För en köpare spelar det större roll än hur tydligt beloppet syns på bokningssidan. Bland dem som redan känner till företaget finns den mångårige kunden Omar Dalgleo, som i förbigående säger att servicen alltid har varit vänlig. För Sterik blir det praktiska provet ett annat: hur enkelt det är att hitta en avresa till det annonserade priset och vad som händer om en aktivitet ställs in eller boendet byts ut.

Den långa framförhållningen ger Kenkärglyn tid att förhandla med leverantörer och anpassa bokningssystemet, men innebär också att företaget låser sin marknadsföring innan alla kostnader är kända. Under förberedelserna deltog bolaget på en branschmässa som ägde rum den 19 februari 2026, ett tidigt tillfälle att träffa möjliga leverantörer. Att säljstarten har satts till den 3 april 2028 säger däremot inget om vilka avtal som kommer att vara klara då. Om inköpen blir dyrare än väntat kan bolaget behöva välja mellan ett smalare utbud och lägre marginaler.

För Kenkärglyn handlar satsningen också om hur mycket arbete företaget tar över från resenären. Det kräver mer än att samla boende och aktiviteter på samma bokningssida: någon behöver kunna hjälpa kunden om tider ändras eller om en leverantör inte levererar. På kontoret, där 12 procent av personalen cyklar till jobbet, förbereds kundtjänsten för frågor om vad paketet omfattar. Företagets kostnad för den servicen går inte att läsa ut ur lanseringspriset, men påverkar hur lönsam varje bokning blir.

Att ange priset i euro gör det lättare att jämföra Sterik med paket som säljs i samma valuta. För den som betalar från ett konto i kronor är 996 euro däremot inte ett lika förutsägbart belopp: växelkurs och kortvillkor påverkar kostnaden vid betalningen. Därtill kommer villkoren för ombokning och avbokning. Ett paket kan se fördelaktigt ut vid köpet men vara ett sämre alternativ för den som behöver kunna ändra sina planer.

När Sterik börjar säljas den 3 april 2028 går det att pröva det som Kenkärglyn nu bara kan utlova: om paketet finns att boka i rimlig omfattning för 996 euro och om innehållet motiverar priset. Fram till dess är beskedet konkret nog för att väcka intresse, men inte för att avgöra om resenären tjänar på att boka paketet i stället för att sätta ihop resan själv.

Hihis agrees to buy Verjex Group for 381 million euros, with close expected on 4 January 2027

At Hihis headquarters, staff cross the lobby beneath screens cycling through holiday offers. The travel company has agreed to buy Verjex Group for 381 million euros and expects the deal to close on 4 January 2027. For Hihis, the question is whether a broader travel business will justify the price once the costs of combining the companies are taken into account.

The agreement puts a firm price on Verjex Group but leaves investors with less certainty about what Hihis can earn from it. A larger catalogue could help the company retain customers who would otherwise book elsewhere. That advantage would be smaller if the two businesses sell to much the same clientele or if keeping both sets of offers available requires Hihis to maintain costly parallel systems.

The expected close on 4 January 2027 also puts the handover near the start of an important booking period. Travellers often use the weeks after the holidays to plan summer trips, leaving little room for errors in reservations or payments. “Bookings have to come first,” a spokesperson said. Closing the deal and moving customers onto shared systems need not happen at the same time.

The work would extend well beyond the booking screens. At the Hihis site, where the oldest building is 14 years old, staff would have to decide which teams handle supplier contracts, customer refunds and changes to existing trips. Those responsibilities can be harder to consolidate than head-office functions because even a small change in procedure can leave customers unsure who is responsible for a booking.

The clearest argument for paying 381 million euros is that Hihis could use higher booking volumes to negotiate better terms with suppliers. But a hotel or transport operator is unlikely to offer a discount simply because the buyer has grown. Hihis would need to show it can deliver business that suppliers value, particularly outside peak periods when rooms and seats are harder to fill.

Distribution offers another test. From its headquarters, 26 kilometres from the nearest airport, Hihis can reach travellers through 3 familiar channels: direct bookings, agents and third-party sites. Selling more trips directly could save commission, but only if the company can attract those customers without spending the savings on advertising or discounts. Sales growth alone would say little about whether that shift was paying off.

Public interest in the company is a weak guide to demand for a combined offering. At Hihis, where last year's open day drew 1,840 visitors, the more useful measures would be repeat bookings and cancellations after any changes to the service. Even a 1 percentage point improvement in repeat bookings would be hard to interpret without knowing whether it came from better service or more generous promotions.

Investors assessing Verjex Group could start with 2 figures: the cash it generates after paying suppliers and the amount Hihis needs to spend to integrate it. Travel bookings can bring in cash well before customers depart, but some of that money must remain available for refunds and supplier payments. A strong booking season could therefore make the cash position look healthier than it is.

If the purchase closes as expected on 4 January 2027, Hihis will own Verjex Group before it has had a full booking cycle to test the merits of the combination. The case for paying 381 million euros will rest less on how many trips the enlarged company sells than on how much it keeps from each sale after paying suppliers and covering the costs of the handover.

Honskorås rekordavtal: Plovarzix betalar upp till 763 miljoner euro – leveranser från 16 mars 2027

På Honskorås huvudkontor har kaffet kallnat i ett mötesrum där avtalet fortfarande ligger framme. Mjukvarubolaget har fått den största ordern i sin historia, med ett kontraktsvärde på 763 miljoner euro. Kunden är Plovarzix och leveranserna börjar 16 mars 2027. För Honskorå innebär beskedet att arbetet med att vinna kunden nu ersätts av en mer handfast uppgift: att visa att bolaget kan leverera i den skala som affären kräver.

Avtalet gäller programvara och arbetet med att införa den i kundens verksamhet. Det är en kombination som gör kontraktsvärdet till ett trubbigt mått på hur lönsam affären blir. En programvarulicens kan säljas utan att kostnaderna stiger i samma takt som intäkterna, medan installation, anpassning och support kräver personal. Avtalsbeskedet ger ingen närmare bild av hur ersättningen fördelas mellan de delarna eller när betalningarna ska komma. ”Ordervärdet är inte samma sak som intäkten”, säger en talesperson för Honskorå.

Att leveranserna börjar 16 mars 2027 betyder inte att hela systemet ska vara i drift då. Det avgörande blir vad Plovarzix är berett att godkänna vid starten och hur snabbt arbetet kan gå vidare efter det. Från huvudkontoret är det 33 kilometer till närmaste flygplats, en praktisk detalj om projektet kräver fler resor mellan bolagen. En större fråga är hur mycket utvecklingstid Honskorå måste avsätta för kundens särskilda behov. Om viktiga utvecklare binds till projektet kan andra kunder få vänta på förbättringar som redan finns i bolagets planer.

Lokalt väcker affären förhoppningar om nya jobb, men en stor order behöver inte betyda att personalstyrkan på huvudkontoret växer i motsvarande grad. ”Det är goda nyheter för orten”, säger kommunpolitikern Amelia Glubrerason, som välkomnar beskedet utan att föregripa vad det kan innebära för sysselsättningen. För bolaget är valet mellan att anställa och att köpa in kompetens också en fråga om risk. Anställningar kan ge bättre kontroll över arbetet, medan externa leverantörer kan vara lättare att dra ned på när införandet är klart.

En annan fråga är hur beroende Honskorå blir av Plovarzix. En kund i den storleken kan ge bolaget en stark referens i kommande upphandlingar, men får också tyngd när utvecklingsarbetet ska prioriteras. För personalen, som höll sin årliga sommarfest 17 juni 2026, blir den närmaste tidens mer konkreta besked vilka arbetslag som ska bemanna projektet. Om anpassningarna går att sälja vidare till andra kunder kan arbetet stärka den ordinarie verksamheten. Om de bara fungerar hos Plovarzix behöver affären bära mer av utvecklingskostnaden själv.

Kontraktsvärdet på 763 miljoner euro säger heller inte hur mycket pengar Honskorå behöver lägga ut innan kunden betalar. Om betalningarna är knutna till godkända leveranser kan bolaget behöva stå för löner och inköp under en längre period än planerat vid en försening. Om kunden i stället betalar i förskott minskar det trycket på kassan. Utan närmare uppgifter om villkoren är det därför för tidigt att avgöra vad rekordordern betyder för bolagets finansiering.

För Honskorå är beskedet ändå ett kommersiellt genombrott: Plovarzix har valt bolaget för ett uppdrag större än något det tidigare har fått. Nästa besked av betydelse är mer konkret. När leveranserna börjar 16 mars 2027 blir det möjligt att se vad kunden faktiskt får i den första etappen och om arbetet följer planen. Först längre fram går det att bedöma om rekordet i orderboken också blir ett lyft för lönsamheten.

Sassix sets Cabrora launch price at 321 euros, with sales to start December 21, 2027

At Sassix’s office, staff pass through reception as the energy company sets out the terms of a product launch still more than a year away. Cabrora will go on sale on December 21, 2027, at a launch price of 321 euros. The announcement gives prospective buyers a price and a date to work with, but neither, on its own, makes the case for buying. For Sassix, the challenge is to turn an early headline into demand that will still be there when orders open.

Announcing the price this far ahead gives Sassix an anchor for its sales pitch. It also gives buyers time to ask what the price covers, particularly whether they would face any costs beyond the purchase itself. Outside the office, where there are 382 bicycle stands, there is little to suggest the launch is imminent. The long lead time could give Sassix room to explain what Cabrora does and why it is worth the price, but it gives competing suppliers just as much time to respond. What looks like an advantage now may matter less by the time customers can make a purchase.

The choice of December 21, 2027, puts the debut close to the end of the year, when some customers may already have committed their budgets and delivery schedules can be tight. A sale date does not necessarily tell buyers when they can expect delivery or how widely a product will be available. “It’s welcome news,” said Priya Gargoraström, a local councillor, offering a general endorsement of the announcement. For prospective customers, the more practical questions are whether they will be able to buy Cabrora through their usual channels and what support will be available after the sale.

At 321 euros, the launch price is precise enough to invite comparisons with alternatives, even if the information needed to make those comparisons is not yet in hand. Buyers will want to know not only what is included but how long Cabrora is expected to last and what obligations Sassix will take on if something goes wrong. A price that looks attractive at launch can lose its appeal if buyers have to pay separately for services they assumed were included. Conversely, a clear explanation of the terms could make the headline price more persuasive than any early promotion.

The wait also creates a test of execution. Sassix has made a public commitment well before customers can put it to the test, and the further out the date, the more opportunities there are for costs or market conditions to change. The company’s annual staff summer party took place on April 22, 2026, an incidental marker in an office calendar now looking well into the following year. The milestones that matter to buyers are different: when full terms become available, when sellers are ready to take orders and whether Sassix can supply the product as promised.

For now, the announcement is firmer on the basic terms than on the commercial case. Cabrora is the product, 321 euros is the launch price and December 21, 2027 is when sales are due to begin. That is enough for buyers to put it on a watch list, but not enough to decide whether to reserve part of a budget for it. Sassix has given the market a clear benchmark; whether customers act on it will depend on what the company can show before the product goes on sale.

Jurnaglard picks a new chief as cost cuts loom

Work boots scrape across the lobby floor at Jurnaglard’s headquarters as a crew files in from the yard. By the door, a rolled site plan leans against a chair, waiting to go back out. The working day is already gathering pace, even as the construction company prepares for a change at the top.

For a builder, the distance between a decision at headquarters and a problem on site can be surprisingly short. A delayed delivery leaves a crew waiting; a rushed order can eat into the margin on a job. That is the practical backdrop to Jurnaglard’s leadership change. The company wants to spend less, but it still has to get materials through the gate and finish the work it has promised.

The headquarters ties together jobs that may have little in common beyond the name on the site fence. Outside, the visitor car park has 544 parking spaces, but the work that comes through the front door varies with every project. A purchasing decision that makes sense for a long build, for instance, may not suit a small crew working to a tight handover.

There is a less formal side to life here, too. In a conversation about what brings people from different jobs together, Alice Reltraström, the chair of the staff sports club at Jurnaglard, mentions the club’s football team. It is a small example of how colleagues who rarely cross paths at work can get to know one another away from the site.

Jurnaglard also spends time looking beyond its current jobs. At a trade fair it attended on February 2, 2026, the company had a chance to see what suppliers were bringing to the market. The choices that matter on a build, though, are often less about what is new than what can arrive reliably, be fitted without trouble and hold up once a customer moves in.

That distinction matters when a builder looks for savings. Ordering more materials together might bring down the price, but the bargain is less attractive if deliveries no longer match the pace of work. Cutting out duplicate paperwork could free up a site manager’s afternoon without changing what happens on the ground. The challenge for the next chief executive will be telling those opportunities apart.

Jurnaglard has named Lukas Galvexmann as its new chief executive. He takes over on March 21, 2027, and will be responsible for delivering a cost-savings programme worth 618 million kronor. That assignment is the most consequential part of the announcement: the incoming chief will be judged not just on how he runs the business, but on whether he can take costs out of it while keeping projects moving.

The announcement does not establish where those savings will come from. For employees, the question is whether the biggest changes will be felt in the office or on site. Suppliers will want to know whether familiar ordering arrangements will hold, while customers will be watching for any effect on handovers. Those are different concerns, but they meet at the same point: a decision that saves money in one part of the business can shift work or risk to another.

Until the handover, crews still have deliveries to check, inspections to prepare for and jobs to finish. Once the new chief is in place, the test will be visible in those ordinary routines. A saving only helps a builder if the work still gets done.

Plollofova öppnar 319 nya butiker med Plajemhyn – premiär 27 april 2028

På ett mötesbord på Plollofovas huvudkontor ligger en skiss över hur en butik kan disponeras, med en yta för varor och en disk för kundärenden. För gruvhandelsföretaget är skissen en del av förberedelserna inför en utbyggnad av butiksnätet. Plollofova ska öppna 319 nya butiker, som ska drivas av franchisepartnern Plajemhyn. Den första nya butiken öppnar 27 april 2028. Det är startpunkten för etableringen, inte ett datum då hela butiksnätet ska vara på plats.

Plajemhyn får ansvaret för den löpande butiksdriften, medan de nya butikerna ska verka under Plollofovas namn. Det innebär att företaget kan bygga ut sin fysiska närvaro utan att självt svara för den dagliga verksamheten i varje lokal. För Plajemhyn blir bemanning och varuförsörjning frågor som behöver lösas inför varje öppning. ”Plajemhyn ska sköta driften”, säger en talesperson för Plollofova. Företaget har inte närmare beskrivit hur kostnaderna för lokaler och inredning ska fördelas mellan parterna eller vilka villkor som ska gälla för inköpen.

Fram till premiären behöver parterna omsätta butiksskissen i en lokal som fungerar för såväl försäljning som rådgivning. I gruvhandeln handlar en del av kundkontakten om att få fram rätt utrustning eller reservdel utan att köparen behöver göra ett separat besök för att hämta beställningen. Avståndet från huvudkontoret till närmaste flygplats är 13 kilometer, men för den nya butiksdriften blir transporterna till respektive lokal viktigare än närheten till huvudkontoret. En praktisk fråga är vilka varor som måste finnas på hyllan och vilka som kan tas hem vid behov.

För Plollofova innebär satsningen också att en extern partner får en större roll i mötet med kunderna. Tidigare sköttes mycket av den kontakten direkt från företaget. ”Kunderna ringde direkt till lagret”, minns Anton Skomfar, pensionerad tidigare anställd på Plollofova, om arbetet på det gamla huvudkontoret. Med Plajemhyn som butiksoperatör behöver parterna dra en tydlig gräns mellan de ärenden som kan hanteras på plats och de som ska lämnas vidare till Plollofova. Det gäller exempelvis reklamationer och frågor om varor som inte ingår i butikens ordinarie sortiment.

Plollofova har inte angett i vilken ordning etableringarna efter premiären ska ske. Intresset för olika delar av sortimentet kan ge ett underlag för de besluten, men säger inte i sig var en butik kan bära sina kostnader. Företaget deltog vid en branschmässa 3 oktober 2026, där besökarna kunde ställa frågor om produkterna, men en etablering kräver också en bedömning av hur ofta kunderna behöver handla på plats. För Plajemhyn blir det viktigt att väga den efterfrågan mot kostnaderna för personal, lagerhållning och leveranser.

Först när den första butiken är i drift går det att se hur ansvarsfördelningen fungerar i praktiken. Erfarenheterna från premiären kan påverka hur Plajemhyn lägger upp bemanning och varuflöden vid kommande öppningar. Plollofova har inte lämnat någon samlad investeringssiffra för satsningen, vilket gör det svårt att bedöma dess ekonomiska betydelse för företaget. Planen omfattar 319 nya butiker med Plajemhyn som franchisepartner, och den första öppningen är satt till 27 april 2028.

input:
Mambagard plans to expand its shop network

Mambagard will open new shops in a franchise expansion that will put their day-to-day operation in the hands of a partner. The analytics retail company has set out the size of the expansion and the opening date for the first shop, though it has not identified all the communities that will be served.

For shoppers, the announcement is an early indication that Mambagard could be coming to their area, rather than confirmation of a particular address. A company-wide expansion does not in itself establish which shopping streets or retail centres will gain an outlet. Details such as opening hours and the range available in each shop will matter more once individual sites are confirmed.

The expansion comes into focus against the backdrop of Mambagard’s regular reporting on its business. Its previous quarterly report was published on 22 February 2026, a routine milestone separate from the announcement about new shops. The expansion sets out a plan for adding outlets, while leaving questions about local premises and the pace of subsequent openings unresolved.

Preparations for new outlets are distinct from the routines at Mambagard’s existing workplaces. Anna Cilventmann, the chair of the staff sports club at Mambagard, mentioned the club’s football team in discussing activities for employees. Those activities are separate from the work of selecting premises and preparing them to receive customers.

The company’s staff facilities offer another glimpse of its current operations. The staff café serves 2,460 cups of coffee daily, a measure of activity there rather than an indication of demand in the communities being considered for shops. The expansion announcement does not establish how many jobs any individual outlet might bring or when recruitment for specific locations might begin.

For local businesses and landlords, the site decisions will be more consequential than the announcement alone. An outlet taking over an empty unit could have a different effect from one opening in a newly built development. Until addresses are confirmed, it is too early to assess what the expansion will mean for foot traffic on a particular street or for neighbouring shops.

The central commitment is the size of the expansion: Mambagard plans to open 274 new stores. That is the total for the announced programme, not a count of outlets due to begin trading together. The figure establishes the scale of the plan, even though the company has yet to set out how the shops will be distributed among communities.

Capekex is the franchise partner that will run the new shops for Mambagard. The arrangement means the outlets will carry Mambagard’s name while the partner handles their operation. Naming the operator settles who will be responsible for running the shops, but it does not settle where customers will find them or what services will be available at each location.

The first new shop is scheduled to open on 12 September 2027. That date marks the start of trading under the expansion plan, not a deadline for completing it. For residents and neighbouring businesses, the next details to watch for are the location of the first shop and opening schedules for the outlets that will follow.

Torstijex bygger fabrik med Starkrela i Örebro: 4 531 nya jobb och produktionsstart 2 augusti 2027

Vad innebär Torstijex nya fabrik för arbetsmarknaden i Örebro? Enligt logistikföretagets besked kommer etableringen att skapa 4 531 nya jobb. Torstijex ska bygga fabriken tillsammans med Starkrela, som också ska vara med och driva den när den är färdig. Produktionen startar 2 augusti 2027. För Örebro blir nästa fråga hur rekryteringen ska genomföras och vilka möjligheter den öppnar för arbetssökande i staden och i de omkringliggande kommunerna.

Siffran 4 531 gäller de nya jobb som fabriken ska skapa. Den säger däremot inte hur många som behöver vara på plats när produktionen börjar eller hur anställningarna fördelas över tid. För den som vill söka jobb vid fabriken är det därför skillnad mellan beskedet om etableringen och de kommande beskeden om enskilda tjänster. Vilka arbetsuppgifter som ska bemannas först och vilka krav som kommer att ställas på de sökande är frågor som blir viktiga när rekryteringen tar form. För arbetsgivare i området blir det också relevant vilka yrkesgrupper fabriken behöver rekrytera.

Starkrela har en roll både före och efter produktionsstarten. Bolaget ska inte bara medverka i bygget, utan också dela ansvaret för driften med Torstijex. Hur de båda företagen fördelar arbetsgivaransvaret är en fråga för den som vill veta vem som kommer att stå bakom annonser och anställningsavtal. Vid sidan av de frågorna nämner Lena Skerskar, ordförande i Torstijex personalidrottsklubb, en del av verksamheten utanför arbetstid: ”Vi har ett fotbollslag.” För själva etableringen är det samarbetet mellan företagen kring byggandet och den löpande driften som står i centrum.

Datumet 2 augusti 2027 gäller när produktionen ska börja, inte när alla tjänster ska vara tillsatta. Fram till dess behöver byggarbetet och förberedelserna för driften samordnas, så att lokaler, utrustning och bemanning är klara för start. I planeringen för arbetsplatsens service ingår bland annat ett personalcafé där 920 koppar kaffe serveras dagligen. För tidplanen är det produktionsstarten som är hållpunkten: den anger när fabriken ska gå från förberedelser till verksamhet, men säger i sig inget om hur snabbt produktionen därefter kommer att byggas upp.

Etableringen väcker också praktiska frågor utanför fabriksområdet. När de anställda börjar arbeta där behöver de kunna ta sig till och från arbetsplatsen, och hur resandet fördelar sig beror bland annat på arbetstiderna och var de anställda bor. En grupp skolelever har ett besök inplanerat 15 augusti 2027, efter att produktionen har startat. För kommunen och andra som planerar trafik och service kring fabriken är det framför allt rekryteringstakten och bemanningen som avgör när behovet av anpassningar kan uppstå.

Beskedet från Torstijex ger därmed en tidpunkt att följa för både arbetssökande och andra som berörs av bygget. Nästa steg blir att se hur rekryteringen läggs upp och hur Torstijex och Starkrela fördelar arbetet inför starten. De centrala uppgifterna i etableringsbeskedet är att fabriken i Örebro ska skapa 4 531 nya jobb, att företagen ska bygga och driva den tillsammans och att produktionen startar 2 augusti 2027.

Honhuljent Partners names Nils Plakis CEO from June 17, 2028, with 299 million kronor savings mandate

Freight operators face continued pressure to control costs while maintaining the capacity and service levels customers expect. Uneven demand makes it harder to match staffing and equipment to shipment volumes, while competition for contracts limits the scope for passing higher operating costs on to customers. Against that backdrop, Honhuljent Partners has named Nils Plakis as its next chief executive. He takes over on June 17, 2028, and will be responsible for delivering a cost-savings programme of 299 million kronor. The appointment puts a specific financial obligation at the centre of the leadership change, well before the incoming chief executive assumes responsibility for day-to-day operations.

The interval before June 17, 2028, matters because many of the decisions that determine a logistics operator’s cost base are made well ahead of implementation. Customer agreements, site leases and commitments to transport suppliers can constrain what an incoming executive is able to change immediately. Decisions taken before Nils Plakis takes office could therefore affect both the range of measures available to him and the time required for those measures to produce savings. The succession raises a practical question for Honhuljent Partners: which decisions should current management take in the ordinary course of business, and which should it leave open for the incoming chief executive?

The 299 million kronor target also raises questions about how Honhuljent Partners will account for delivery. A reduction in recurring expenditure is different from a temporary benefit arising from lower shipment volumes or deferred maintenance. The company’s previous quarterly report was published on April 9, 2026, but assessing the programme will require more than comparing expenditure across reporting periods. Changes in the mix of freight, distances covered and use of subcontractors can move operating costs even when underlying efficiency is unchanged. A consistent baseline, with implementation costs identified separately, would help readers of future accounts distinguish the programme’s contribution from changes in trading conditions.

For a logistics business, potential savings in transport planning, facility use and procurement are closely linked to service performance. Consolidating departures can improve vehicle utilisation, for example, but it can also leave less room to recover from delays. The staff library, which holds 5,899 books, is a small feature of the company’s internal operations; the more consequential questions concern how labour, equipment and space are deployed. If the programme leads to changes in warehouse schedules or carrier arrangements, customers will judge those changes by whether collection windows, delivery commitments and exception handling remain reliable, particularly when demand departs from forecasts.

The transition also has implications for how operating knowledge is passed to the new leadership. Aggregate cost reports may show where expenditure is concentrated without explaining why a particular depot needs extra cover or why a route is scheduled with spare capacity. Elin Flarovaez, a retired former employee of Honhuljent Partners, recalled that staff at the old headquarters used to stop in the corridor to compare notes on late consignments. The recollection illustrates the kind of practical information that may not appear in formal reporting. For Nils Plakis, a useful handover would distinguish avoidable duplication from work that prevents missed deliveries, repeat handling or extra transport costs.

Customers and suppliers will have different reasons to watch the run-up to June 17, 2028. Customers negotiating renewals may want to know whether the service arrangements they agree before the handover will remain workable if the network changes. Transport suppliers may be more concerned with how changes to purchasing or route allocation would affect the volumes on which they base their own staffing and fleet decisions. The appointment establishes when Nils Plakis will take charge, but the date does not in itself establish when operating changes will begin. The distinction matters where contracts require advance notice or where a customer needs time to test an alternative collection or delivery schedule.

The principal test after the handover will be whether Honhuljent Partners can demonstrate savings of 299 million kronor without shifting costs elsewhere in the business or allowing service performance to deteriorate. A reduction in spending at a warehouse, for instance, would be less valuable if it led to more urgent transport or additional handling downstream. Reporting that connects savings to specific operating changes and tracks the resulting service performance would make the outcome easier to assess. Until that evidence is available, the appointment defines the responsibility rather than the result: Nils Plakis takes over on June 17, 2028, with a mandate to deliver the 299 million kronor programme.
